abstract: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for learning reusable knowledge from graphstructured data. Unlike conventional graph neural networks (GNNs), which are usually trained for a specific graph and task, GFMs aim to transfer graph representations across graphs, tasks, and feature modalities. However, the established literature is rapidly fragmenting in different directions. In this tutorial, we divide current GFM research into five predominant families and explore them appropriately. We first introduce the motivation for GFMs and the high-level taxonomy that organizes the area. We then discuss five representative families: LLM-Enhanced GNNs, GNN-Enhanced LLMs, Unified Graph Models, Graph Mixture-of-Experts, and Graph Prompt Learning illustrating their individual strengths which underpin their current design. Finally, we outline future research directions from a data management perspective. This tutorial will help researchers and practitioners from the database and data management community understand the major implementation paths and open problems in Graph Foundation Models.

title: Craw: A Unified and Efficient Querying Framework for Large-Scale Video Datasets.
abstract: The ubiquitous deployment of cameras has led to explosive growth of video data, creating an urgent need to explore valuable content. Single-level queries are insufficient to extract comprehensive information, raising the demand for multi-level queries (existence, dynamic, similarity) within a single unified system. However, limited by the high complexity and redundancy of video, existing systems usually support single-level queries, while Vision-Language Models that support multi-level queries incur prohibitive computational overhead, making them infeasible for large-scale video datasets. To address these issues, we propose Craw, a framework for efficient multi-level queries on large-scale video datasets. Specifically, Craw (1) designs the Video Semantic Unit to encapsulate video semantics, (2) develops a semantic-preserving video segmentation algorithm, and (3) constructs a hybrid index framework integrating an inverted index with a cluster index layer for efficient query execution. Experimental results show that Craw outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) by reducing query latency up to two orders of magnitude, while effectively supporting multi-level queries.

title: A Semantics-aware Approach for Graph Edit Distance Estimation over Knowledge Graphs.
abstract: Graph Edit Distance (GED) is a key metric for measuring the similarity between two Knowledge Graphs (KGs), deﬁned as the minimum number of atomic operations required to transform one KG into another. It has broad applications in ﬁelds such as pattern recognition, biological analysis, and graph databases. The state-of-the-art approaches adopt Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to predict GED, but they are limited to simple graphs and cannot be directly applied to the KGs, as they fail to capture the rich semantics and complex relationships present in KGs. To design a KG-native solution, in this paper, we propose a semantics-aware GNN model, SEABED, to capture local semantic dependencies and global semantic consistency between two KGs. Extensive experiments on four real-world KGs demonstrate that our proposed algorithm outperforms the stateof-the-art methods on all datasets. In particular, the mean absolute error is reduced by up to 66.7%, while the accuracy is improved by up to 70.5%, without increasing the computation time.

title: LiBox: A Learned Index as an Array to Minimize Last-Mile Search.
abstract: Learned indexes have attracted significant attention for their potential to deliver substantial performance and space savings over traditional index structures. Their advantage lies in replacing explicit key comparisons with model-based computation that predicts the position of a search key in a sorted array. However, prediction errors prevent models from precisely locating keys, requiring a last-mile search over a candidate range. Both model evaluation and last-mile search can be expensive, limiting the performance. We propose LiBox, a hierarchical, box-based learned index that overcomes these limitations. LiBox partitions a sorted key array into “boxes” such that: (1) the box containing a search key can be identified with zero error using a simple linear regression function, and (2) the last-mile search within a box requires only a single AVX-512 instruction. This design yields a highly predictable and efficient lookup, with each query involving a fixed, minimal number of instructions and memory accesses. By allocating modest extra space within each box to handle irregular key distributions, LiBox supports both read and write queries at near array-access speed. Furthermore, its reorganization operations can be aligned with workload read/write intensity, enabling high-performance reads while hiding structural modification costs. We propose LiBox, a hierarchical box-based learned index that addresses these limitations. LiBox partitions a sorted key array into disjoint “boxes” such that: (1) the box containing a search key can be identified without error using a simple linear regression function, and (2) the last-mile search within a box usually requires only a single AVX-512 vector instruction. This design yields a highly predictable and efficient lookup process, with each query involving a fixed and minimal number of instructions and memory accesses. By allocating a modest amount of additional space within each box to accommodate irregular key distributions, LiBox supports both read and write queries at near–array-access speed. We implemented LiBox and conducted an extensive experimental evaluation. The results demonstrate that it significantly outperforms both state-of-the-art learned indexes (e.g., ALEX, LIPP) and non-learned indexes (e.g., ART) while achieving comparable or better space efficiency.

title: DBCooker: A Database Kernel-Specialized Coding Agent Harness.
abstract: Database kernels continuously incorporate new built-in functions to support diverse applications. Synthesizing these native functions is highly complex, as it requires identifying multiple internal units, placing them in the correct source files, and reusing specific internal references. Although recent advancement in LLM-based coding agent frameworks (harnesses) exhibit superior capability, they are typically general-purpose and struggle with the massive and highly coupled database kernel repositories. To address this, we demonstrate DBCooker, a database kernel–specialized coding agent harness. DBCooker offers three core functionalities: (1) Kernel Dependency Inspector, which enables users to inspect internal units and cross-file references via hybrid declaration collection, distinctive unit identification, and cross-unit reference analysis; (2) Interactive Synthesis Planner, which constructs high-level implementation plans through progressive code synthesis and three-stage code validation, allowing developers to verify and refine plans before execution; and (3) Progressive Debugging Workspace, which integrates with database-specific pipelines to provide efficient feedback and adaptive repair, powered by techniques such as operation-astool abstraction and memory-augmented orchestration. Conference attendees will experience how DBCooker seamlessly transforms high-level SQL function requests into validated, kernel-ready code for mainstream databases (e.g., SQLite, PostgreSQL, DuckDB).

title: DBAIOps: A Reasoning LLM-Enhanced Database Operation and Maintenance System using Knowledge Graphs.
abstract: The operation and maintenance (O&M) of database systems is critical to ensuring system availability and performance, typically requiring expert experience (e.g., identifying metric-to-anomaly relations) for effective diagnosis and recovery. However, existing automatic database O&M methods, including commercial products, cannot effectively utilize expert experience. On the one hand, rulebased methods only support basic O&M tasks (e.g., metric-based anomaly detection), which are mostly numerical equations and cannot effectively incorporate literal O&M experience (e.g., troubleshooting guidance in manuals). On the other hand, LLM-based methods, which retrieve fragmented information (e.g., standard documents + RAG), often generate inaccurate or generic results. To address these limitations, we present DBAIOps, a novel hybrid database O&M system that combines reasoning LLMs with knowledge graphs to achieve DBA-style diagnosis. First, DBAIOps introduces a heterogeneous graph model for representing the diagnosis experience, and proposes a semi-automatic graph construction algorithm to build that graph from thousands of documents. Second, DBAIOps develops a collection of (800+) reusable anomaly models that identify both directly alerted metrics and implicitly correlated experience and metrics. Third, for any given anomaly, DBAIOps employs an automatic graph exploration mechanism that explores the relevant paths over the graph and dynamically explores potential gaps (missing paths) without human intervention. Based on the explored diagnosis paths, DBAIOps leverages reasoning LLM (e.g., DeepSeek-R1) that inputs the relevant pathways, identifies root causes, and generates clear diagnosis reports for both DBAs and common users. Our evaluation over four mainstream database systems (Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and DM8) demonstrates that DBAIOps outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, 34.85% and 47.22% higher in root cause and human evaluation accuracy, respectively. DBAIOps supports 25 database systems and has been deployed in 20 real-world scenarios, covering domains like finance, energy, and healthcare (https://www.dbaiops.com).

title: Bridging NL2SQL for CAN Signal Analytics at NIO: From Externalized Schemas to CTE Pipelines.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) promise natural-language access to data, yet applying them to Controller Area Network (CAN) signal SQL analytics in the automotive industry is challenging. First, CAN data warehouses store tens of thousands of signals as opaque numeric columns. Multiple signals are often packed into a single column as bit segments, requiring external Database CAN (DBC) files beyond the native database schema for proper definitions. Second, engineers’ natural-language queries often use terms that map to multiple signals in the DBC files, with little direct indication of which signals are being referenced. Finally, signal analysis in production involves multi-step SQL pipelines using layered Common Table Expressions (CTEs) for tasks such as temporal alignment, more complex than those handled by existing NL2SQL methods. To address these, we present NIO-Weaver, an end-to-end CAN signal analytics system within a graph-augmented multi-agent framework. First, to uncover signals hidden in opaque numeric columns, we introduce an automated graph-construction pipeline that leverages DBC files to build a domain-knowledge graph, associating signals with potential high-level terms. Second, to bridge the semantic gap between natural-language queries and multiple signals, we propose an optimized retrieval method that extracts terms from queries and performs hybrid retrieval. We combine regex matching, embedding search, and constrained graph traversal to identify candidate signals for further processing. Finally, to simplify the generation of multi-step CTE-based pipelines, we introduce a hierarchical generation paradigm. We decompose queries into plans, incrementally generating executable CTEs, while self-correction mechanisms refine missing signals and incorrect SQL. Experiments on the real-world industrial CAN warehouse at NIO demonstrate that NIO-Weaver outperforms baselines by up to 67.2%.

title: Narwhal: Breaking the Local Boundary via Disaggregated Memory Scheduling for Alibaba AnalyticDB.
abstract: Cloud OLAP workloads are bursty and memory-hungry. Per-machine DRAM caps and co-scaled CPU/memory provisioning are fragile. They lead to low utilization, slow autoscaling, and transient OOMs. Prediction-driven schedulers and bin-packing optimizers mitigate but struggle with rigid per-machine memory boundaries and forecasting errors, Existing RDMA or OS-level remote-memory approaches either assume single-tenant trusted clusters (lacking hardware isolation and QoS) or treat remote DRAM as opaque swap. We present Narwhal, an RDMA-co-designed analytical database. It jointly schedules local DRAM and a shared remote memory pool to trade consolidation against bounded remote borrowing. It enforces hardware-level multi-tenant isolation with per-tenant RDMA Protection Domains, quotas, and QoS. It uses a database-aware memory allocator with a three-tier cache and a pressure-threshold invariant to avoid OOMs and protect metadata. Integrated into a production engine, Narwhal eliminates OOMs, boosts memory overselling from 92.67% to 121.89% (+29.22) and node utilization from 78.16% to 96.63% (+18.47), while limiting average remote memory borrowing to just 1.63%.

title: SuperDRI: Graph-Guided Autonomous Troubleshooting for Cloud Databases.
abstract: We demonstrate SuperDRI, an autonomous troubleshooting system for large-scale cloud databases such as Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse. Incident diagnosis requires expert, multi-step reasoning across heterogeneous telemetry and tools, while much of this knowledge remains scattered across documentation and senior engineers’ experience. Rather than relying on manually authored playbooks, SuperDRI learns structured troubleshooting workflows directly from historical incident traces through a multi-agent extraction pipeline, incrementally building InvestiGraph, a typed workflow graph of database problems, diagnostic actions, and causal relationships for each domain. At runtime, an agentic graph-traversal mechanism explores InvestiGraph, generates and executes readonly Kusto (KQL) queries against database telemetry, and iteratively reasons over results to reach mitigations. The system further incorporates real-time feedback learning, allowing database engineers to inject domain knowledge into the graph. We illustrate four capabilities: (1) exploring a production-scale InvestiGraph learned from over 1,300 real incidents (10,000+ nodes), (2) observing autonomous troubleshooting with adaptive KQL generation and execution against Fabric DW telemetry, (3) editing the graph and observing how feedback immediately improves subsequent runs, and (4) accessing SuperDRI through multiple MCPcompatible clients. SuperDRI is deployed in production at Microsoft for Azure Data incident management.

title: Highly-Efficient Large-Scale k-means with Individual Fairness.
abstract: Traditional 𝑘-means minimizes the sum of squared error (SSE) but may treat data points unequally, as some are assigned to significantly distant centroids. This leads to unfair outcomes in downstream tasks such as facility location planning, where each cluster corresponds to a specific share of limited resources. To address this, we modify the objective of 𝑘-means via exponential tilting, which emphasizes the impact of distant data points and yields a new objective: the tilted SSE. We propose TKM, which optimizes via coordinate descent and stochastic gradient descent, and improves fairness by shifting centroids toward underrepresented groups. We adopt the within-cluster variance to quantify fairness among individuals within the same group, which provably reduces extreme disparities in outcomes. To improve efficiency, we propose FastTKM, which uses stochastic dynamics to estimate the tilted SSE with lower computational cost. We theoretically demonstrate that, under our proposed methods, the variance decreases with 𝑡, a scaling factor that controls the degree of centroid deviation. Furthermore, our methods exhibit time and space complexities comparable to the classical Lloyd’s heuristic. Experimentally, our methods outperform six baselines in terms of clustering utility and fairness across twelve real-world datasets. In terms of efficiency, our methods achieve thousand-fold speedups in running time and reduction in memory usage, with this factor growing as the dataset size increases.

title: RNSG: A Range-Aware Graph Index for Efficient Range-Filtered Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search.
abstract: Range-filtered approximate nearest neighbor (RFANN) search is a fundamental operation in modern data systems. Given a set of objects, each with a vector and a numerical attribute, an RFANN query retrieves the nearest neighbors to a query vector among those objects whose numerical attributes fall within the range specified by the query. Existing state-of-the-art methods for RFANN search often require constructing multiple range-specific graph indexes to achieve high query performance, which incurs significant indexing overhead. To address this, we first establish a novel graph indexing theory, the range-aware relative neighborhood graph (RRNG), which jointly considers spatial and attribute proximity. We prove that the RRNG satisfies two crucial properties: (1) monotonic searchability, which ensures correct nearest neighbor retrieval via beam search; and (2) structural heredity, which guarantees that any rangeinduced sub-graph remains a valid RRNG, thus enabling efficient search with a single graph index. Based on this theoretical foundation, we propose a new graph index, called RNSG, as a practical solution that approximates RRNG efficiently. We develop fast algorithms for both constructing the RNSG index and processing RFANN queries with it. Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets show that RNSG achieves significantly higher query performance with a more compact index and lower construction cost than existing state-of-the-art methods.

title: Quiver: Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in GPU-SSD ANNS
abstract: Billion-scale Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) increasingly adopts a GPU-SSD architecture, where GPU fetches and processes fine-grained, SSD-resident data on-demand. However, since GPUs lack native support for I/O scheduling, existing ANNS systems are trapped in a severe throughput-latency tradeoff. They either delegate scheduling to best-effort host drivers, achieving high throughput but suffering severe latency inflation due to interference, or poll I/O completion directly inside the kernel, which achieves low latency but starves GPU utilization. This paper demonstrates that this tradeoff is not fundamental. Our key insight is that ANNS exhibits strict per-hop performance predictability in both computation and I/O, which can make scheduling lightweight enough to be onloaded directly into the GPU kernel. We thus present GPipeANN, which deterministically and lightly switches among multiple query contexts at hop boundaries to achieve perfect compute-I/O overlap. Evaluations on billion-scale datasets show GPipeANN shifts the Pareto frontier, achieving high throughput and low latency simultaneously. GPipeANN is available at https://github.com/ruc-system/GPipeANN.

title: Efficient Training on Multiple Consumer GPUs with MovingPipe
abstract: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on consumer-grade GPUs is highly cost-effective, yet constrained by limited GPU memory and slow PCIe interconnects. Pipeline parallelism combined with CPU offloading mitigates these hardware bottlenecks by reducing communication overhead. However, existing PP schedules suffer from an inherent limitation termed the weight binding issue. Binding uneven model stages (e.g., the LM head is large) to GPUs limits the pipeline’s throughput to that of the GPU with the heaviest load, leading to severe pipeline bubbles. In this paper, we propose RoundPipe, a novel pipeline schedule that breaks the weight binding constraint on consumer GPU servers. RoundPipe treats GPUs as a pool of stateless execution workers and dynamically dispatches computation stages across devices in a round-robin manner, achieving a near-zero-bubble pipeline. To ensure training correctness and system efficiency, RoundPipe integrates a priority-aware transfer scheduling engine, a Layerwise Model Consistency Protocol, and an automated layer partitioning algorithm. Evaluations on an 8 × RTX 4090 server demonstrate that RoundPipe achieves 1.48–2.16 × speedups over state-of-the-art baselines when fine-tuning 1.7B to 32B models. Remarkably, RoundPipe enables LoRA fine-tuning of the Qwen3-235B model with 31K sequence length on a single server. RoundPipe has been open-sourced as a Python library. Project Page: https://thustorage.github.io/RoundPipe/

title: Make Graphs Great Again: Rethinking LLM Agent Architecture via Structure-Semantic Separation
abstract: LLM-centric agent architectures route each observation back to the model for the next decision, leaving control logic implicit in a growing prompt and forcing repeated reconstruction of task state and routine execution progress even when runtime evidence determines the next transition. We present structure–semantic separation as a control boundary for LLM agents, making recurring tool-use structure explicit and executable while reserving the model for semantic decisions that structure cannot resolve. MotifAgent realizes this boundary through executable motif graphs: the Structure Engine advances graph execution based on runtime evidence, while the Semantic Engine resolves semantic gaps through scoped LLM calls, making recurring tool-use structure executable runtime state rather than prompt guidance. Exposing motif progress to the serving backend additionally enables structure-aware scheduling and fine-grained KV-cache retention. Across APIBank, TauBench, and AppWorld, MotifAgent reduces LLM calls and token consumption while maintaining comparable task performance. Serving replay experiments further show reduced prefill-stage latency and improved admission-time KV reuse under the evaluated queueing and cache-pressure conditions.

title: Demystifying the Performance of Kernel-Bypass TCP Stacks
abstract: Kernel-bypass TCP stacks (uTCPs) typically deliver several-fold higher throughput and an order of magnitude lower tail latency than in-kernel TCP (kTCP), yet their performance advantages still lack comprehensive and systematic explanation. Existing analyses with side-by-side benchmarking and profiling fail to identify and disentangle individual factors’ contributions, as stacks differ in many aspects simultaneously. This paper instead conducts an iterative ablation study that identifies performance factors from uTCPs and reproduces them in kTCP one by one to estimate their contributions. Focusing on small-message RPC scenarios, we identify 11 such factors that jointly close the 3.81 × per-request processing time gap between kTCP and the fastest uTCP to within 5%, while also achieving comparable latency. Our study reveals that uTCPs benefit most from feature specialization (closing 49% of the gap): they shed stack functionality such as security hardening and protocol completeness, resulting in reduced instruction count. Meanwhile, uTCPs apply architectural improvements (closing 35% of the gap) by achieving better data locality and scheduling for higher execution efficiency. The remaining implementation optimizations close the final 16% of the gap. Notably, kernel-bypass itself is neither sufficient nor necessary: eliminating syscall overhead accounts for only \({\sim }5\%\) of the gap, and all identified factors can be reproduced within the kernel. Overall, no single factor dominates the gap. Crucially, most contributors involve a deployment tradeoff: uTCPs gain speed by sacrificing generality, security, or resource sharing.

title: Understanding and Detecting Performance Regressions in Modern Open-Source Server Applications
abstract: Modern open-source server applications evolve rapidly through frequent code updates, which can introduce performance regressions that gradually degrade application efficiency. Traditional benchmark testing is often too expensive to run after every commit and can miss regressions that manifest only under specific workloads. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive study of 98 real-world performance regressions across 11 widely used open-source systems. We find that many regressions stem from small, seemingly innocuous commits and are triggered only through rarely exercised execution paths. Guided by these insights, we develop Scalpel, a practical performance regression detection tool for large open-source server applications. The core idea is to turn each code change into a targeted regression check: Scalpel reduces benchmark cost by selecting only test cases that reach changed code, and exposes workload-specific regressions by exploring commit-relevant paths, ranking candidate paths with instruction counts, and confirming slowdowns through native re-execution. Our evaluation shows that Scalpel detects 24 of 30 known regressions in our benchmark set. It also exposes 25 new regressions, 12 of which have been confirmed by communities. Across recent commits, Scalpel spends 62 minutes per code-modifying commit on average, achieving 3.5–13 × speedup over official benchmark testing.

title: Skip it, don't speed it. Accelerating Graph Pattern Matching through Disjoint Intersection Bypassing
abstract: Set intersection dominates the inner loop of graph pattern matching (GPM). Practical engines repeatedly intersect sorted adjacency lists under irregular memory access and tight latency constraints, and many issued intersections produce no output. Our workload characterization shows that these disjoint intersections are common, especially under symmetry-breaking constraints. Prior work accelerates exact intersection kernels and prunes search states. Disjoint intersections nevertheless remain in the measured workload, leaving an opportunity to certify emptiness before exact execution. This paper presents GraphDIB, a Disjoint Intersection Bypassing mechanism for GPM. GraphDIB stores a cacheline-sized 512-bit signature per vertex neighborhood and tests two signatures with a single SIMD bitwise AND, where a zero result certifies disjointness and safely skips the exact intersection kernel. To maximize bypass coverage under this fixed metadata budget, GraphDIB learns a workload-specific projection from sampled disjoint intersections. We define false positive penalty to quantify how strongly pairs of vertices should map to different signature bits, use it to refine the projection iteratively, and extend the guard to symmetry-breaking constrained intersections through projection-aligned reordering. Across 16 workload instances, GraphDIB improves end-to-end performance by 1.56 × geomean and up to 6.84 × over the fastest evaluated baseline, while reducing executed intersections by \(30.2\%\) on average and preserving the original exact intersection kernel.

title: MoECatch: Efficient Checkpointing and Consistent Recovery for Mixture-of-Experts Models
abstract: Checkpointing is essential for fault-tolerant large language model training, but it increasingly limits persistence frequency and recovery efficiency as training runs become longer and clusters become larger. This problem is especially acute in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) systems, where checkpoint bytes are dominated by expert parameters and optimizer states. Conventional checkpointing persists all experts uniformly at every checkpoint, even though expert updates are highly uneven under skewed token routing. This mismatch wastes checkpointing bandwidth on persisting “barely changed experts”, limits attainable checkpoint frequency, and increases rollback cost after failures. To address this mismatch, we present MoECatch, a sparse checkpointing system for MoE training that treats sparse checkpointing as a coupled checkpoint-and-recovery problem. On the checkpoint path, Aging-then-Greedy Expert Selection (AGES) prioritizes which experts to persist under a fixed budget. On the recovery path, Version Catch-Up (VCU) reconstructs stale experts from mixed-version checkpoints while leaving already aligned state unchanged. MoECatch further accelerates recovery through minimum executable-state restoration and asynchronous optimizer staging. We implement MoECatch in the MindSpeed framework. The results show that MoECatch improves attainable checkpoint frequency by up to 2.5 × and reduces end-to-end wasted time after failures by up to \(22.86\%\). Across both pre-training and fine-tuning workloads, recovery preserves average downstream-task accuracy relative to full-checkpoint recovery. At the state level, the relative L2 parameter deviation between the recovered model and the same-iteration full checkpoint does not exceed \(0.001\%\).

title: Unipool: Efficient Management of Pre-Provisioned Resources for Container Platforms
abstract: Cloud platforms reduce deployment latency by pre-initializing resources, but fragmented resource management across cloud layers often leads to substantial over-provisioning and increased cost. Through production trace analysis and replay using state-of-the-practice resource management approaches, we show that independently managing resources at each layer results in a poor trade-off between resource waste and deployment latency. We present Unipool , the first unified platform that exposes the state of pre-provisioned resources across layers, enabling more accurate resource pool sizing and dynamic multiplexing. Guided by insights from production traces, Unipool leverages cloud-native workload patterns to safely consolidate and oversubscribe pre-provisioned resources, significantly reducing platform cost while preserving quality of service. We implement Unipool on Kubernetes and Kata Containers, and evaluate it using both a large-scale event-driven simulator and a testbed of 25 virtual machines. Across mixed Function-as-a-Service and Container-as-a-Service production traces, we reduce resource waste by 92% while lowering container deployment latency by 21% compared with state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Courier: Host-Transparent Direct Network I/O for Secure Containers in Cloud VMs
abstract: Secure containers strengthen isolation by encapsulating conventional OS-level containers within lightweight virtual machines (microVMs), and have been widely adopted to execute untrusted, multi-tenant workloads in modern cloud platforms. In practice, these platforms are increasingly deployed atop cloud virtual machines to exploit cloud elasticity and cost efficiency, which places secure containers within a nested virtualization stack. Although prior work has significantly advanced nested CPU and memory virtualization, network I/O remains a critical bottleneck. Existing para-virtualized networking solutions incur substantial overhead due to repeated cross-layer mediation, while hardware-assisted device passthrough depends on IOMMU virtualization support that is often unavailable in public clouds. This paper presents Courier, a direct network I/O architecture that enables passthrough-like, high-performance networking for secure containers in cloud environments. Courier rethinks nested network virtualization by introducing an in-guest shadow IOMMU to enable secure device passthrough with a shorter network stack and zero-copy data transfer, without requiring host involvement. In addition, Courier incorporates several data-plane techniques, including direct-kick notifications, used-ring passthrough, and efficient interrupt handling, to further improve packet processing efficiency. We implement Courier in a production system and evaluated it using both microbenchmarks and real-world applications. The results show that Courier significantly improves both throughput and tail latency, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art virtio-net and vhost-net by up to 9.36x and 96.7%, respectively, while achieving near-native performance under realistic workloads.

title: SeaStore: Redesigning Ceph’s Storage Backend for CPU-Efficient NVMe Performance
abstract: This paper presents SeaStore, a new CPU-efficient, NVMe-oriented storage backend for Ceph, a general-purpose distributed storage system. Over the past decade, Ceph has evolved alongside advancements in storage technology. However, it faces fundamental challenges in random I/O performance due to the structural limitations of its software stack that cannot be addressed via the modular changes adopted in the past. Addressing these limitations requires solving three design challenges: (1) the limitations of a heterogeneous and tightly coupled RocksDB-based architecture, (2) the lack of efficient per-core transaction processing, (3) maintaining high transaction concurrency without excessive contention. SeaStore efficiently overcomes these limitations by introducing three techniques: sharding with hybrid layout, cooperative optimistic pipeline processing, and contention reduction via structure-free updates. We have completely rebuilt the storage backend and integrated SeaStore into the Ceph mainline as a next generation storage backend. Our evaluation results show that SeaStore achieves up to 70% improvement in small random write performance, and scales IOPS with the number of cores. Furthermore, it offers at least 2x higher IOPS under mixed workloads and serves small random reads while reducing CPU usage by 25%.

title: Breaking Host-Wide Blocking: Boundary-Closure SCSI Error Handling
abstract: Linux SCSI Error Handling (EH) in modern storage systems frequently causes excessive host-wide blocking and prolonged fault-resolution duration. Our observations reveal that recovery durations range from tens of seconds to minutes, stalling healthy devices across the entire host even when faults remain localized, which conflicts with the bounded response-time requirements of modern applications. To mitigate these limitations, we propose a boundary-closure SCSI error handling (BC-EH) mechanism, which infers the minimal necessary recovery boundary from SCSI topology, forward progress loss (FPL) evidence, and driver capability constraints, and then confines blocking, validation, and recovery actions to that boundary. In contrast to existing Linux SCSI EH, BC-EH decouples fault-boundary inference from recovery execution, preventing unnecessary recovery escalation beyond the inferred fault boundary. We implement BC-EH in Linux kernel 6.18 and evaluate it across multiple SCSI drivers and storage backends. Experimental results demonstrate that BC-EH achieves up to a 9.9× reduction in fault-resolution duration and shortens Kafka JBOD error handling activity windows by 3.7×, while showing no statistically significant steady-state performance bias (0.04% signed mean difference).

title: EvoFuzz: IR-Aware Fuzzing for JIT Compilers through the Lens of Node Evolution
abstract: JIT compilers are core components of modern language virtual machines, and their bugs can crash the VM or silently miscompile programs. Modern JIT compilers perform multiple rounds of optimizations on graph-based intermediate representation (IR), where each round modifies, transforms, or eliminates IR nodes (referred to as node evolution). Bugs arise when the combination of multiple evolution paths violates inherent constraints of the IR. However, existing fuzzing tools lack fine-grained awareness of IR-level node evolution and struggle to construct the compound IR structures required to trigger such evolution, limiting their ability to explore the evolution combination space effectively. We propose EvoFuzz, an IR-aware fuzzing framework for Java virtual machine (JVM) JIT compilers, comprising three components: Node Mutators, which induce IR nodes of different semantic categories through source-level mutations and are portable across compilers; Evolution Profiling, which tracks evolution at the optimization-path granularity and defines a set distance metric as the feedback signal for fuzzing; and Combination-Aware Scheduling, which learns sequential dependencies among mutators via Markov dependencies to optimize mutator selection. We implement EvoFuzz as a practical fuzzing system for production JVMs and evaluate it on multiple versions of OpenJDK HotSpot, OpenJ9, and GraalVM. EvoFuzz discovered 45 bugs, of which 37 have been confirmed and 10 have been fixed by developers. Compared with state-of-the-art JVM fuzzers, EvoFuzz improves code coverage in the HotSpot C2 compiler module by approximately 7%, triggers 1.7–1.9 × as many unique optimization paths on average, and achieves 3.0–3.5 × the baselines’ median set distance at 12 hours. These results show that node-evolution-aware feedback is an effective signal for exposing correctness bugs in production JIT compilers.

title: SplineFS: Adaptive Learned Directory Indexing for Memory-Constrained Filesystems
abstract: Local filesystems manage increasingly large namespaces under limited directory-index cache. When this working set no longer fits, namespace walks suffer repeated dcache misses and directory-index probes before reaching file data. A learned index can reduce this overhead by replacing explicit routing metadata with a compact model that maps a lookup key to a small candidate range. However, applying learned indexing to filesystem directories is non-trivial: mutations change the key-to-record mapping and can force model maintenance, while parent-scoped lookup fragments the namespace into small keysets that duplicate models and leave little search to save. We observe that namespace mutations cluster in space and operation order, so large, stable subtrees are the right unit of learned indexing. We present SplineFS, a filesystem that promotes a quiet subtree into one shared learned index, amortizing the model across its directories while avoiding frequent retraining. An append-only delta absorbs occasional mutations, and sustained churn triggers demotion to the conventional layout, so SplineFS does no harm where locality is absent. Implemented in ext4, SplineFS reduces directory metadata by up to 19.7 × and improves cold-scan throughput by up to 3.6 × on real namespaces, and speeds real application stages by up to 2.1 ×.

title: XCG: Decoupling Control from Configuration to Improve Cgroup Scalability with Flat Mapping
abstract: Cgroup (control group) is the Linux kernel mechanism that underpins resource management for containers, a foundational building block of modern cloud systems. A cgroup combines a core, which maintains hierarchical configuration and process-controller mappings, with resource controllers, which enforce limits on the connected processes. This coupled design provides flexible resource management, but it serializes cgroup creation and process attachment through coarse-grained kernel synchronization, compromising scalability when launching many short-lived containers simultaneously. Existing pooling-based mitigations move cgroup creation off the startup path but do not remove the underlying cost: pools must be provisioned for bursts, can miss during spikes, and add management overhead. We observe that serverless platforms typically organize processes into per-container groups and enforce resource limitations at the granularity of individual containers, and thus there is no correlation between processes across different containers. Based on this observation, in this paper we present XCG, a novel extension to cgroup for improving its scalability. The basic idea of XCG is to decouple control (by the controllers) from configuration (by the core), allowing container startup to involve only the creation of controllers for predefined resource usage control, while avoiding the creation of the core. The removal of cgroup core enables flat process-controller mapping, i.e., directly attaching the processes to the controllers, which allows XCG to use fine-grained locks to protect cgroup operations thus effectively improving scalability. XCG further reduces controller setup cost through lazy release and on-demand initialization, and streamlines configuration by extending cgroupfs with an ioctl interface that batches creation and configuration into a single operation. We have implemented XCG on Linux kernel v6.7.2. Extensive evaluation shows that XCG significantly outperforms the original cgroup design when launching a large number of containers in parallel.

title: Premature Hardware Binding is the Root of all Evil! Making Serverless Performance-Portable with Lazy Hardware Binding
abstract: Modern clouds are characterized by increasing hardware heterogeneity. While exposing hardware complexity to developers enables performance optimizations, it also constrains deployment options and fragments the platform’s resource pool. Conversely, serverless platforms abstract hardware details to increase deployment flexibility. However, this forces developers to compile their applications conservatively to ensure portability, sacrificing significant performance gains of CPU-specific instruction set extensions. To break through this tradeoff, we introduce Mosaic, a serverless platform that decouples portable application logic from performance-critical dependencies. Rather than eagerly bundling applications into a single binary, Mosaic delays binding until the deployment target is known, dynamically injecting pre-compiled, hardware-optimized library implementations tailored to the specific machine. The proposed design offers deployment flexibility, near-optimal performance, and low developer burden. Our evaluation demonstrates that Mosaic matches the throughput of aggressively optimized CPU-bound applications, achieving up to 40% higher throughput than builds without CPU-specific optimizations. Simultaneously, its cross-architecture portability prevents cluster fragmentation, reducing 90th percentile end-to-end scheduling latencies by up to 604 × under constrained resources, while its architectural deduplication reduces application storage footprints by over two orders of magnitude.

title: FlexMARL: Graph-Driven Rollout-Training Co-Design for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Despite algorithm-level innovations for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), the underlying infrastructure for large-scale MARL remains underexplored. Existing training frameworks primarily optimize for single-agent scenarios and fail to capture the graph-structured nature of MARL. This fundamental mismatch leads to three MARL-specific challenges: topology-induced rollout skew, critical path synchronization barriers, and dynamic training demand. To bridge this gap, we propose FlexMARL, a graph-driven rollout-training co-designed framework for large-scale LLM-based MARL. FlexMARL introduces the multi-agent execution graph (MEG) and materializes the intermediate representation as the MEG Store, which provides decentralized multi-table storage and serves as the data hub for system components. Built around the MEG Store, the Rollout Engine develops dependency parallel sampling with hierarchical load balancing, which reduces inference latency and balances intra-agent/inter-agent loads. The Joint Orchestrator exploits an agent-level asynchronous pipeline to mitigate the critical path synchronization barriers while maintaining consistency. The Training Engine achieves on-demand resource allocation by collectively managing training processes for individual agents. The training states of different agents are swapped via location-agnostic communication APIs. Empirical results on a production cluster demonstrate that FlexMARL achieves up to 7.3 × speedup and improves hardware utilization by up to 5.6 × compared to existing frameworks.

title: Storage Evolution for Exascale Supercomputers: Lessons from Sunway TaihuLight to OceanLight
abstract: Modern supercomputers are transitioning from homogeneous to heterogeneous architectures supporting mixed HPC, AI, and HTC workloads. However, traditional storage design assumptions, single schedulers, static load balancing, and pure write optimization are failing under this new paradigm. This paper presents a longitudinal analysis of eight years of production data from two generations of Sunway supercomputers: TaihuLight and its exascale successor, OceanLight. Analyzing 10 million jobs and 60 TB of I/O traces, we reveal several counterintuitive bottlenecks: scheduler congestion from HTC bursts; Round-Robin load balancing that trades reduced interference frequency for more severe degradation and collapsed cache locality; the burst buffer dilemma where write gains come with read variability; and write-read asymmetry where write-optimized layouts cause severe post-processing slowdowns. Building on these findings, we implement and evaluate two mitigation mechanisms on OceanLight hardware: token-bucket traffic shaping and domain-aware forwarding scheduling. We also discuss design principles for coordinated burst buffer draining, load-aware dynamic mapping, and layout-aware I/O guidance as future directions. These insights offer actionable guidance for designing next-generation supercomputers that efficiently support converged mixed workloads.

title: Bypassing Android System Services for Fast UI Responsiveness: A Kernel-Application Co-Design Approach
abstract: Android’s input and display paths rely heavily on user-space system services (InputFlinger, SurfaceFlinger), which introduce significant inter-process communication and scheduling overhead, leading to high latency and limited scalability. We present a method that bypasses these system services by splitting their functionality between the Linux kernel and individual application processes. In the kernel, a Screen Manager module directly dispatches input events and composites display buffers; within each process, dedicated memory segments and shared libraries allow unmodified apps to consume input and submit frames without involving any user-space service. This kernel-application co-design eliminates redundant IPC and context switches from the critical path. Our prototype on Android 14 reduces end-to-end input latency by 90.91% and display latency by 87.93%, while also lowering CPU and memory usage, and significantly improves scalability as the number of concurrent apps increases. All source code is publicly available.

title: Plurio: Scaling Microkernel-based Operating System via Service Localization and Memory Pooling
abstract: Microkernel-based operating systems offer strong isolation but often scale poorly on multicore platforms due to expensive IPC. We present Plurio, a microkernel-based operating system architecture that revisits service organization and memory management around two principles: localizing service execution and pooling memory resources. Plurio selects among pre-generated service combinations at runtime to turn frequent cross-service invocations into local function calls, and employs a global memory pool that exposes physical memory as capabilities for mapping in a shared virtual address space. Affinity-aware worker arrangement and proxy-managed request caches further shorten communication path and reduce data copying. We implement Plurio on the Genode framework and evaluate it with Filebench and YCSB on x86 and ARM platforms. For the evaluated metadata-intensive workload, Plurio improves throughput over unmodified Genode by up to 1.9 × on x86 and 1.8 × on ARM, demonstrating the benefits of service localization within these multicore configurations.

title: Beyond Target Placement: Unified Multi-Objective Path-Aware Offline VM Scheduling at Scale
abstract: Offline scheduling of virtual machines (VMs) in large-scale cloud clusters faces three core challenges: uniformly modeling heterogeneous business objectives, efficiently solving NP-hard problems at industrial scale, and producing feasible migration paths rather than merely computing target placements. This paper presents PAMOS (Path-Aware Multi-objective Offline Scheduling), an offline scheduling system built around a unified modeling framework that abstracts diverse constraints and objectives into a single additive cost minimization problem through several composable cost forms. A domain-specific language (DSL) enables non-expert users to define rules in fewer than ten lines of code. At the solving level, a heuristic algorithm combining active and passive migration mechanisms directly produces feasible migration-path sequences. SVD-accelerated Tag-based Cost computation and a level-cache mechanism meet the minute-scale planning-time service-level objective (SLO). Evaluation on 631 production problems shows that, after path construction, three placement-based baselines realize only 14.7–20.3% of PAMOS’s optimization effectiveness and retain only 10.3–13.6% of their proposed migrations. At the scale where exact comparison is feasible, PAMOS achieves 97.0% of the path-aware mixed-integer programming (MIP) solver’s optimum with four orders of magnitude speedup. PAMOS has run stably at Alibaba Cloud for over eight years, processing thousands of tasks daily, achieving substantial cost reductions and stability improvements.

title: EMDedup: Accelerating DLRM via In-Network EMbedding Layer Deduplication
abstract: DLRM systems are highly dependent on the efficiency of the embedding layer, which becomes increasingly critical as it scales trillions of parameters, causing the model’s memory footprint to exceed the HBM capacity of a single GPU node. Consequently, DLRM is scaled out by sharding the embedding layer across multiple nodes for distributed inference and training, shifting the bottleneck to all-to-all communication over fast interconnects such as RDMA and CXL. Prior works addressed the challenge with fine-grained hybrid parallelism that uses DP for caching hot embeddings. However, for TB-scale DLRM with multi-hot sparse features, caching proves neither cost-effective nor efficient to address the communication bottleneck. Our insight shows that 1) deduplication achieves comparable communication volume reduction to caching under large global batch sizes, without persistent embedding replication, and 2) as DLRM s scale out across many nodes, there is a non-trivial fraction of cross-node duplicated sparse feature requests, which can be identified by in‑network deduplication. Motivated, we propose EMDedup, a host-network co-designed system accelerating distributed DLRM training and inference, which offloads request deduplication and multicast to programmable switches, while also incorporating existing in-network gradient aggregation to further improve DLRM training. Its customized end-host communication backend enables in-network functions to operate transparently with existing DLRM frameworks and embedding parallelisms. Real testbed results show that EMDedup reduces communication and embedding overhead, achieving average speedups of 1.74x and 1.94x in training and inference runtime over PyTorch DLRM systems, while our large‑scale simulations also have similar results.

title: Cold-Patching for Faster Edit-Compile-Run Cycles
abstract: Programmers rely on fast edit-compile-run cycles when debugging code, exploring unfamiliar codebases, and trying out new ideas. Fiddle is a new tool for cold-patching small changes onto large compiled software systems. When repeatedly editing a small number of compilation units, Fiddle is faster than linkers, uses less memory, and does not require saving intermediate compilation artifacts. Fiddle is simpler and more reliable than hot-patching because it does not need to deal with global state migration or non-quiescent functions. Fiddle is designed for developers repeatedly fiddling with a handful of functions in a large codebase; it cannot patch changes to the types of global non-static objects, it cannot patch binaries compiled with LTO, and its speed relies on repeatedly editing the same set of compilation units. We end by describing a suite of tools enabled by the Fiddle cold-patching primitive that make it easier to rapidly prototype modifications to compiled system software.

title: FDP-Rocks: An Effective Use Case of FDP in RocksDB
abstract: While Flexible Data Placement (FDP) presents a promising opportunity to reduce device-level write amplification (DLWA) in SSDs, using this feature effectively remains challenging. A major obstacle is that the effectiveness of FDP still relies on accurate data lifetime characterization. As RocksDB is a dominant data management system powering many data center services and already provides built-in FDP support, it serves as an ideal case study. In this work, we demonstrate that RocksDB’s native level-based file placement, an intuitive and seemingly unmistakable design choice, ironically leads to unexpected data misplacement and is ineffective at reducing DLWA. To address this, we present FDP-Rocks, a system designed for effective FDP use in RocksDB by leveraging ML-model-based file lifetime classification and a custom SSTable compaction candidate selection policy to unlock the full potential of FDP. We implement FDP-Rocks in RocksDB. Experiments on diverse workloads demonstrate that FDP-Rocks can improve overall throughput by up to 37% and reduce DLWA by up to 43% over RocksDB with FDP enabled.

title: HYPIC: Position-Independent Caching for Hybrid-Attention LLM Serving
abstract: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agentic LLM serving, prompts are assembled from multiple independent segments into long contexts, making prefill dominate the computation cost. To reduce this cost, position-independent caching (PIC) admits KV reuse for non-contiguous segments across requests, while hybrid-attention models reduce computational complexity using linear attention. However, existing PIC methods break down on hybrid-attention models because their per-token KV-cache reuse primitives do not transfer to per-request recurrent states. In this work, we present Hypic, the first system to accelerate hybrid-attention LLM serving with position-independent caching. For linear-attention layers, we identify the segment-cumulative transition operator as the missing algebraic primitive and cache it for each segment, enabling near-exact and constant-time state composition. For the remaining full-attention layers, we construct a small seam window to propagate hidden states through the linear-attention layers, so that cross-segment attention can be repaired by recomputation. Finally, Hypic introduces segment parallelism, which parallelizes cache-miss prefill across instances, turning long cold requests into an accelerable workload. Evaluated across four hybrid-attention models and five workloads, Hypic reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 3.25 × on average and improves QPS by 1.66 × over Prefix Cache, while preserving task quality with a 1.71-point gap from Full Recompute.

title: CoreCapture: Anomaly-Aware System Trace Sampling for Resource-Constrained Mobile Devices
abstract: Diagnosing performance anomalies on production mobile devices requires System Traces, which are whole-system runtime records spanning kernel, services, and applications. Yet each trace dump consumes over 100 MB, and the daily upload budget shared across all diagnostic components limits collection to a few dumps per day; anomalies occurring after the quota is exhausted are permanently lost. We present CoreCapture, an on-device system that compresses each dump by filtering out steady-state data while preserving anomaly-relevant diagnostic context. CoreCapture employs a dual-stream anomaly detector (DS-TraceNet) that separately models semantic and temporal features to identify anomalous traces, followed by a spatio-temporal retention mechanism (STA-ER) that expands each anomaly to a complete interaction-event window and prunes irrelevant threads. Evaluation on production traces shows that CoreCapture reduces per-dump volume by approximately 70% while preserving 95% event-level anomaly coverage. Deployed on production smartphones, it adds only 4–5% CPU and 13–15 MB memory overhead on device per alert-triggered dump. Our source code demo and two data cases are publicly available at https://github.com/linjiaxiaoyue/CoreCapture.

title: Rattan: An Extensible and Scalable Modular Internet Path Emulator
abstract: Modern transport and application innovations require evaluation over fast, heterogeneous, and dynamic Internet paths. Existing emulators do not simultaneously provide the expressiveness to model complex paths, the efficiency for high-throughput and concurrent experiments, and the scalability for large evaluation campaigns. We present Rattan , a modular Internet path emulator that separates path expression from execution. Users compose cells, each implementing one path effect, into channel graphs. A graph-aware runtime executes these graphs using metadata-oriented packet I/O and graph-aware scheduling, while a manager and orchestrator provision isolated channels across machines. Our evaluation demonstrates significant throughput improvement, efficient execution of complex path compositions, and dense concurrent emulation with stable results. A multipath case study shows that Rattan can reveal changes in performance rankings missed by other emulators. Deployment at a large CDN provider further demonstrates sustained pre-deployment evaluation and production extensibility. After integration into its workflow, the average congestion-control rollout cycle decreased from 24 weeks to 18 days.

title: AccFS: An Accelerator-Aware File System for Non-Volatile Memory
abstract: We present AccFS, a novel non-volatile memory (NVM) file system designed to exploit hardware accelerators, such as Intel Data Streaming Accelerator (DSA), on modern CPUs. To better leverage DSA, AccFS decouples space allocation from persistence and employs core-local data management, enabling temporal and spatial coalescing of requests issued to DSA. Furthermore, AccFS coordinates data-movement and integrity-protection operations between CPU cores and DSA using insight-driven scheduling policies. We implement AccFS in the Linux kernel and evaluate it on a 64-core machine equipped with Intel DSA and Optane DC persistent memory module (DCPMM). The experimental results show that AccFS achieves up to 2.71 × higher throughput and 108.71 × lower latency than seven NVM file systems while reducing CPU utilization by up to 84.99%.

title: brg-pk: A Practical Verified High-Throughput Kernel Lock for OpenBSD
abstract: Operating system kernels make extensive use of locks to handle concurrent accesses to shared data, hence the efficiency of kernel lock mechanisms is crucial to system performance. In this paper we present a new locking algorithm, brg-pk, its verification, and an empirical evaluation. As a result of our efforts brg-pk is the default kernel lock (mutex) implementation in OpenBSD. The algorithm uses concepts of barging and parking from current practice and adapts them for use in a cross-platform operating system kernel. Our empirical analysis is focussed on behaviour under various workloads corresponding to those experienced by the OpenBSD kernel, and we find that brg-pk overall outperforms five established lock algorithms across four different architectures. Much of its performance comes from having a relatively weak fairness guarantee: it is a “mostly-fair” algorithm that sometimes allows threads waiting to acquire the lock to be overtaken. Both experimental and real-world evidence suggest this does not manifest as a problem on the workload profile of the OpenBSD kernel. Given its importance in the kernel, we rigorously verify the correctness of the core algorithm underlying brg-pk via machine-assisted theorem proving; additionally, we validate correctness of the brg-pk implementation via a combination of testing and model checking. Weak memory effects are taken into account in a generic way to support portability across different software and hardware models.

title: HybridQC: Hardware-Grounded Simulation of Tightly Integrated Hybrid Quantum-Classical Systems
abstract: Hybrid quantum–classical performance depends on how quantum processors share classical compute, controllers, memory, and communication links. Circuit simulators and provider measurements expose kernel and job behavior, but leave topology-level questions about controller bottlenecks, quantum capacity, and mixed-workload contention unanswered. We present HybridQC, a discrete-event simulator for configurable hybrid compute units (HCUs). Users specify resource graphs containing classical compute, memory, controllers, quantum annealing (QA) and digital quantum computing (DQC) devices, and links. Jobs become dependent stages for preparation, quantum execution, transfers, reconstruction, and postprocessing. Finite capacities and selectable scheduling policies determine where stages wait and overlap. Service profiles use measurements from D-Wave Advantage 1 and Advantage 2 and IBM Kingston, Marrakesh, and Fez, separating physical quantum-processor occupancy from cloud wall time. Mean absolute percentage errors are 3.92%–8.04% for D-Wave access time and 5.26%–19.01% for IBM quantum seconds. Balanced 10 × HCU scaling improves makespan by 2.19 × –3.42 × , while policy choice changes makespan by 1.80 × for a mixed workload with 20 jobs per workload family. Scaling depends on which inputs grow: 100 × data growth yields median runtime near 306 s, while 100 × joint growth in circuits, shots, and depth reaches 4.806 × 107 s on the fixed HCU. HybridQC enables designers to study topology, scheduling, and workload growth before tightly integrated quantum–classical machines exist physically.

title: ESROS2: Application Sandboxes for Secure ROS2
abstract: ROS2 is a popular middleware for several robotics platforms. It allows rapid prototyping of distributed robotics applications via a convenient publish/subscribe-based abstraction for application communication. Secure ROS2 (SROS2) is a set of patches to ROS2 that provides several basic security primitives to secure application communication, such as encrypted communication and limiting applications to only publish/subscribe to topics that are declared in a manifest. Unfortunately, SROS2 is limited in its ability to confine application communication. Applications can freely communicate with each other by bypassing the SROS2 API and directly making system calls via the underlying operating system. This paper introduces ESROS2, which provides application sandboxing in SROS2. ESROS2 confines applications by limiting the set of system calls that they can issue at runtime. When an application issues a system call, ESROS2 determines whether the context in which the system call was issued is safe, and only then permits the system call to be issued. We describe the design of ESROS2 and its implementation using extended Berkeley Packet Filters (eBPF) and commodity intra-process memory isolation hardware (Intel MPK). We show that ESROS2 works on off-the-shelf application binaries, and effectively enforces application sandboxing while only imposing a modest performance overhead.

title: Resi-DINC: Resilient Distributed In-Network Computing with Closed-Loop Runtime Assurance
abstract: Distributed In-Network Computing (DINC) deploys application logic across programmable network devices, but existing frameworks lack integrated Day-2 operational assurance for runtime disturbances such as device/link failures and service-level agreement (SLA) violations. We present Resi-DINC, an automated closed-loop framework built around an integer linear programming (ILP)-guided multi-expert architecture. An ILP oracle generates expert demonstrations for two-phase deep reinforcement learning (DRL) training—general pre-training and deployment-specific fine-tuning—yielding scenario-specific experts for fault recovery and SLA assurance. At runtime, detected anomalies trigger the corresponding expert, which produces a re-planning decision within milliseconds and drives automated data-plane re-deployment. We evaluate our prototype on Fat-Tree and wide-area network (WAN) backbone topologies. Resi-DINC achieves near-ILP decision quality, with average optimality gaps under 8% for fault recovery and under 7% for SLA assurance, while reducing closed-loop response time by over 480 × and over 150 × , respectively, compared with the manual baseline at the largest evaluated timing scale for each scenario.

title: Spectra: Bandwidth-Faithful Data Placement for Tiered Memory
abstract: Tiered memory systems rely mainly on page-table (PT) scanning or precise event-based sampling (PEBS) to track memory accesses and guide data placement. The tracked accesses are used to quantify data hotness and reflect how intensely data accesses memory. However, we find that the accesses observed by PT and PEBS are not equal to the accesses that reach physical memory, because the cache hierarchy filters and hides the interaction between cores and memory. PT observes accesses before the cache hierarchy and intercepts cache hits that never touch memory. PEBS typically samples LLC misses, so it overlooks prefetches and requests for ownership. This mismatch matters because the performance of tiered systems is increasingly bandwidth-bound, while existing tracking methods do not faithfully reflect the bandwidth consumed by data. We observe 20% to 30% slowdowns in state-of-the-art systems for modern applications. We present Spectra, a tiered memory system that places data by actual memory access intensity (AMAI), the rate at which each object transfers cachelines between the cache hierarchy and physical memory. AMAI counts exactly what physical memory serves. It excludes cache hits that mislead PT and includes the hidden traffic missed by PEBS. Ranking objects by AMAI therefore enables bandwidth-faithful placement. The difficulty is that memory traffic arrives mixed with no provenance. Spectra first builds an analytical model that decomposes the mixed traffic into semantically distinct request classes, each induced by a distinct architectural mechanism. Then each class is attributed to its originating objects through the signal exposed by the corresponding mechanism. Finally, a two-regime policy places data by the recovered AMAI, maximizing aggregate bandwidth utilization. In our evaluation, Spectra reduces execution time by 14.26%–17.45% over the best baseline on memory-intensive applications.

title: Towards High-Throughput Collective Communication via Harnessing PCIe and Dedicated Interconnects
abstract: Collective communication libraries (CCLs) for distributed LLM training focus mainly on dedicated high-speed interconnects and leave PCIe bandwidth under-exploited. For PCIe-only machines, they model collectives as GPU-to-GPU communication and create redundant traffic in the CPU-rooted PCIe hierarchy. For machines with dedicated interconnects, they either ignore PCIe or use a static multipath split that cannot react to runtime PCIe interference. This paper presents HyLink, a two-layer collective communication framework that unlocks PCIe bandwidth and aggregates it with dedicated interconnects. PCIe CCL makes this hierarchy explicit and uses host memory as an active routing point. It expresses topology-aware schedules in a CPU-driven DSL and executes them with an auto-pipelined runtime on GPU copy engines. Multipath Orchestrator splits each collective between the dedicated link and PCIe, and uses runtime feedback to rebalance the split under PCIe interference. In our evaluation across different PCIe-only topologies, PCIe CCL improves large-message collective bandwidth by 26.2% on average over NCCL and reduces Megatron-LM iteration time by 6.1%–6.6%. On the Ascend platform with dedicated interconnects, Multipath Orchestrator improves large-message collective bandwidth by 10.4% on average over HCCL and reduces Megatron-LM iteration time by 2.3%–4.6%.

title: Efficient Strict Serializability for Stateful Serverless Workflows via Workflow Reconciliation
abstract: Serverless computing, represented by Function-as-a-Service (FaaS), is increasingly adopted for deploying complex applications via stateful workflows. However, the lack of strong consistency (i.e., strict serializability) transaction support hinders its broader applicability. Existing solutions are inadequate, either offering only weak consistency or suffering severe performance degradation from concurrency control models that blindly retry requests after conflicts. We therefore present FaaSRep, a high-performance serverless framework that provides strict serializability through workflow reconciliation, which resolves conflicts by learning dependencies from an optimistic execution and using them to guide an organized retry. FaaSRep builds dependencies at validation time, using the validator’s global access view without extra execution-path communication. It further uses a hybrid optimistic/pessimistic protocol to preserve correctness when application-level aborts invalidate the learned order. To reduce the cost of reconciliation, FaaSRep re-executes only affected functions and uses placement information from the initial execution to establish a peer-to-peer fast path during retry. Compared with state-of-the-art systems on real-world applications, FaaSRep improves average throughput by 1.44–2.73 × over Concord and 3.81–9.01 × over Beldi.

title: Schedules Are Solvable Symbols: Tuning-Free Compilation of Tile Programs on Dataflow Architectures
abstract: Modern AI and HPC accelerators increasingly expose dataflow features: software-visible mechanisms for data movement and overlap, such as inter-core communication through the on-chip network and intra-core asynchronous pipelining. These features shift scheduling responsibility from hardware to the compiler, and—because placement, movement, and synchronization become software-visible—they also make the performance of static schedules predictable. Yet high performance on such hardware still relies on vendor-engineered kernel libraries or profile-based auto-tuning, whose embedded expert knowledge transfers poorly across architectures and algorithms. We present Loom, a tuning-free symbolic compiler framework for tile-based SPMD programs on spatial dataflow architectures. The central idea is to treat tile-based SPMD compilation as a hardware-explicit static optimization problem. Loom enumerates discrete spatial-mapping and communication candidates while keeping value parameters—such as tiling factors and pipeline knobs—symbolic within each candidate. From an explicit hardware description, it derives symbolic legality constraints and latency expressions, formulates one CP-SAT problem per schedule candidate, and jointly solves inter-core dataflow, intra-core asynchronous scheduling, and block sizes at compile time. Evaluated on two generations of Tenstorrent hardware (Wormhole/Blackhole), Loom achieves geometric-mean speedups of 0.99 × /1.16 × on GEMM, 2.29 × /2.15 × on Flash Attention, and 1.01 × /1.17 × on Flash Decode. These results suggest that hardware-derived symbolic compilation provides a retargetable alternative to profiling-based tuning for spatial dataflow architectures while remaining interpretable by keeping optimization decisions traceable to source-level symbols.

title: HeadFlow: Scaling Long-Context Training with Head-Group Activation Residency
abstract: Training generative models on long contexts is increasingly bottlenecked by attention activation GPU residency: activations must be on GPU when they are produced and later reused, yet keeping all of them resident limits context length. This paper presents HeadFlow, a runtime system that recasts attention activation management as a head-group lifetime planning problem. HeadFlow exploits a long-context asymmetry: attention compute grows rapidly with sequence length, while each head group’s activation state grows much more slowly, creating windows that can hide movement. It names semantic activation slots, places them across CPU pinned memory, direct GPU–SSD storage, staged GPU–CPU–SSD paths, or recomputation, and executes the resulting plan with asynchronous save, staged prefetch, and load. We implement HeadFlow by extending FlashAttention-compatible operators with plan-aware asynchronous activation movement, and evaluate it across long-context language and multimodal generative training. On text workloads, HeadFlow trains with 512K–1M-token contexts. Its throughput is 1.33 × –1.67 × that of state-of-the-art sequence- and context-parallel baselines. To our knowledge, HeadFlow is the first system to train a 24B model with full parameters at 1M context on only eight 96GB H20 GPUs. On image and video workloads, the same runtime extends the maximum trainable effective tokens by 4.0 × and achieves a 1.32 × speedup. Loss and attention-gradient checks confirm that these gains come from exact activation management rather than approximate attention or lossy execution.

title: Lightweight Memory Tracing via General Binary Analysis and Offline Reconstruction
abstract: Memory tracing is an important technique used in hardware design, debugging, system analysis, and memory management. However, tracing many complex applications is impractical due to the high runtime overhead of existing tracing techniques, typically over 30 ×. This slowdown is especially problematic when tracing one component of a complex system disrupts the execution of the whole system (e.g., a microservice deployed in a datacenter). PTracer is a general binary-level memory tracing tool that reduces tracing overhead by at least an order of magnitude compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Its novel approach breaks tracing into three stages: general static analysis to identify the minimal amount of information required to reconstruct the complete trace, runtime instrumentation to log the information, and offline reconstruction of the memory trace. PTracer can dynamically attach to and detach from running programs, making it more feasible to deploy PTracer in production systems. It has two modes: one optimized for high fidelity and another sacrificing a minor amount of accuracy for better performance. Furthermore, it effectively handles JIT-compiled programs such as JavaScript and Java. Evaluated across diverse benchmarks written in C, Python, Rust, JavaScript and Java, the two modes of PTracer achieve 6 × and 3 × runtime overhead on average, respectively, while state-of-the-art techniques incur 31 × to 152 × overhead on average.

title: eGoT: enhanced graph-of-thoughts for multi-hop knowledge retrieval and hypothesis generation in biomedicine
abstract: Abstract Motivation Research on biological mechanisms and disease processes is limited by fragmented findings across unstructured text in publications. Question answering and hypothesis generation that can reason across multiple sources can overcome this limitation. However, Large language models (LLMs) are prone to inaccuracies and lack clear provenance to primary evidence. Retrieval augmented generation approaches that have provenance to the original source of evidence address these shortcomings. However, the response richness is dependent on the retrieval process design. Current approaches often fail to produce responses requiring multi-hop reasoning across multiple domains. Results To address this, we propose eGoT, which combines automated knowledge graph construction from biomedical literature with a novel graph-of-thoughts approach to query the knowledge base and construct comprehensive responses to natural language questions. Given a corpus of documents, eGoT first uses an LLM-based pipeline to identify and normalize entities and relationships and constructs graph and vector databases. Given an input question, eGoT performs multi-round LLM-based querying of the databases to construct a response. Benchmarking on datasets like MultiHopRAG, HotpotQA, and Ultradomain demonstrates eGoT’s superiority over state-of-the-art retrieval methods, including HopRAG, SireRAG, HiRAG, and HippoRAG. We demonstrate eGoT on two biomedical use cases: (i) generate responses to domain expert-curated questions on small cell lung cancer using 1046 PubMed Central publications, and (ii) demonstrate eGoT’s ability to find plausible connections between Lupus and climate factors (UV exposure) that affect disease trajectory. Availability and implementation https://github.com/NNeuralDynamics/eGOT.git.

title: LAML-Pro: joint maximum likelihood inference of cell genotypes and cell lineage trees
abstract: Motivation Recent dynamic lineage tracing technologies use genome editing to induce heritable mutations, or edits, that accumulate across successive cell divisions. These edits are measured using single-cell sequencing or imaging, providing data to reconstruct cell lineages at single-cell resolution. Current computational approaches to infer cell lineage trees, or phylogenies, from these data perform two separate steps: (1) Identify each cell’s edits (genotype) from the raw sequencing or imaging data; (2) Infer a cell lineage tree from the cell genotypes. However, genotyping cells is an inexact process and genotype errors can yield an inaccurate lineage tree. For example, using fluorescence based-imaging to measure edits results in a high fraction (≈ 25-50%) of uncertain or erroneous genotypes. Results We introduce Lineage Analysis via Maximum Likelihood with PRobabilistic Observations (LAML-Pro), an algorithm that jointly infers cell genotypes and a cell lineage tree. LAML-Pro is based on the Probabilistic Mixed-type Missing Observation (PMMO) model, which we derive to describe both the genome editing and genotype observation processes. LAML-Pro constructs lineage trees from thousands of cells in under an hour by leveraging the sparsity of transitions under the PMMO model. On simulated data, we demonstrate that LAML-Pro corrects genotype errors and infers substantially more accurate trees than existing methods which are vulnerable to genotype errors. Applied to data from two recent imaging-based lineage tracing systems, LAML-Pro reduces genotype errors by 5-fold and produces more spatially coherent lineage trees compared to existing methods. Availability and Implementation LAML-Pro is freely available at: github.com/raphael-group/LAML-Pro.

title: NPBIP: predicting binding preferences of uncharacterized nucleic-acid-binding proteins
abstract: Abstract Motivation Nucleic-acid-binding proteins (NBPs) are crucial regulators of gene expression, recognizing specific RNA or DNA binding sites. While high-throughput experiments have generated vast amounts of binding data, a significant challenge remains in predicting binding affinities of a novel query NBP to any nucleic-acid sequence. Current computational methods often require prior experimental data for the query NBP or are limited to predictions over predefined short RNA or DNA sequences. Results We present New Protein Binding Intensity Predictor (NPBIP), a new method to predict the binding of a query NBP to any RNA or DNA sequence by integrating two complementary components: (i) a similarity-based method that computes a weighted mean of binding predictions over the training NBPs; and (ii) a deep-learning model that combines a large protein language model with a hybrid convolutional-transformer network to predict binding directly. We trained and evaluated NPBIP on 420 RNA-binding protein (RBP) experiments and 464 DNA-binding protein (DBP) experiments. NPBIP significantly outperformed each of its components and all competing baselines, achieving a mean Pearson correlation of 0.414±0.20 and 0.581±0.22 over the RNA- and DNA-binding experiments, respectively.
