Its production relies on the efficient conversion of biomass into syngas. Therefore, this study proposes a bio-methanol production process employing catalytic pyrolysis as the main syngas production step. Specifically, CO2-assisted catalytic pyrolysis was employed because of its higher syngas productivity than conventional catalytic pyrolysis, as reported previously. Building on this approach, three strategies were developed with distinct syngas production routes: Strategy A (catalytic pyrolysis in N2 condition), Strategy B (catalytic pyrolysis in CO2 condition), and Strategy C (integrating biogas reforming with CO2-assisted catalytic pyrolysis). Subsequently, comprehensive energy, economic, and environmental (3E) analyses were performed. The levelized cost of the product (LCOP) of bio-methanol in Strategies B (677 USD/ton) and C (574 USD/ton) was lower than that in Strategy A (830 USD/ton), confirming the economic benefit of CO2-assisted catalytic pyrolysis. Particularly, Strategy C achieved the lowest LCOP, indicating that integrating biogas reforming further improves the economics of bio-methanol production. The sensitivity and uncertainty analyses confirmed the economic reliability of Strategy C, with the LCOP of its bio-methanol comparable to the commercial bio-methanol (320–740 USD/ton). Furthermore, the life cycle assessment (LCA) demonstrated that the bio-methanol produced via Strategy C was environmentally-benign. Overall, these findings highlight Strategy C as a promising option for sustainable bio-methanol production and a viable pathway toward the decarbonization in the international shipping sector.

title: Context-dependent associations between benthic macroinvertebrate diversity and toxic metal(loid) lability: Field evidence from human-impacted river networks
abstract: Toxic metal(loid)s, as hazardous materials, pose persistent ecological risks due to their toxicity, non-degradability, and potential remobilization. Despite the capacity of specific benthic taxa to regulate metal(loid) bioavailability, the community-level role of benthic macroinvertebrates in modulating metal(loid) mobility and ecological risks, particularly in anthropogenically impacted plain river networks, remains poorly understood. Here, we elucidated the interplay between toxic metal(loid)s (As, Cd, Cr, Cu, Ni, Pb, and Zn) and macroinvertebrate communities under complex environmental conditions at 61 sites across four seasons in the Chaohu plain river network by using the diffusive gradients in thin films (DGT) technique and a benthic survey. Total concentrations of most toxic metal(loid)s exceeded background levels by 27%–158%, with higher DGT-labile concentrations of most toxic metal(loid)s observed in summer. Benthic macroinvertebrate diversity was strongly associated with toxic metal(loid) mobility potential (p < 0.001), with its standardized effect exceeding that of most individual physicochemical factors. Notably, this biotic association exhibited a pronounced nonlinear response along environmental gradients. The moving window analysis further indicated that higher metal(loid) loading and ionic strength strengthened the positive association between benthic macroinvertebrate diversity and toxic metal(loid) mobilization. Our findings suggest a context-dependent association between benthic macroinvertebrate communities and toxic metal(loid) mobility, highlighting the need to incorporate sediment contamination and hydrochemical conditions into risk screening for biodiversity-oriented restoration and sustainable management of human-impacted river networks.

title: Nonlinear associations of urban factors with electric ride-hailing charging demand: An XGBoost-SHAP approach
abstract: With the widespread rollout of electric ride-hailing (ERH) vehicles in Chinese cities, high-frequency operating vehicles suffer from queuing delays and substantial time costs during energy replenishment. Although existing research has investigated charging behaviors of electric vehicles and taxis, few studies analyze the associated factors and their nonlinear characteristics underlying charging behaviors of ERH vehicles. This study constructs an interpretable machine learning framework integrating XGBoost and SHAP, based on 1.13 million ERH orders, 1261 public charging stations, built environment, and meteorological data collected in Chongqing, China, during November 16th to 22nd, 2020. The framework identifies predictive association factors and threshold characteristics of ERH charging demand across weekday and weekend scenarios at daily and hourly scales. The results show that XGBoost outperforms random forest and LightGBM in fitting performance, with R2 values of 0.950, 0.907, 0.665, and 0.555 across four scenarios. ERH charging demand is temporally complementary to order demand and spatially more concentrated. Built environment contributes most to charging demand, accounting for 85.35%, 72.49%, 66.17%, and 58.18% of total importance. Distance to CBD, population density, average charging fee, slow chargers count, and fast chargers count exhibit clear nonlinear threshold patterns. Weekday charging demand is more closely related to commuting-oriented operations, while weekend patterns are smoother and more sensitive to weather conditions. These findings provide empirical support for staggered charging guidance and refined public charging infrastructure deployment. However, the applicability of the relevant findings still requires further validation when extended to other cities.

title: Stakeholder-informed feasibility of circular economy strategies in the residential sector: Evidence from Australia
abstract: Circular economy (CE) strategies are increasingly proposed for the built environment; however, their practical implementation in the residential sector remains uncertain. This study evaluates the perceived feasibility and implementation readiness of CE housing strategies in the Australian residential sector using stakeholder-informed thematic analysis. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 24 experts across the residential construction value chain, including designers, builders, policymakers, and industry stakeholders. Using the ReSOLVE framework as a typology of strategies, the analysis identifies four governance-conditioned domains influencing CE implementation: regulatory, economic, technical/infrastructure, and socio-cultural conditions. Based on these findings, the study develops an indicative, governance-conditioned feasibility landscape for CE housing strategies. The findings suggest that the implementation readiness of CE strategies is shaped less by technical availability alone than by how well each strategy aligns across the four governance-conditioned domains. Strategies associated with operational performance, such as energy efficiency and passive design, appear more implementation-ready, whereas material circularity and closed-loop resource flows remain more constrained by unresolved regulatory, economic, technical/infrastructure, and socio-cultural barriers. These barriers are understood as systemic because they require coordinated changes across policy, markets, infrastructure, industry practice, and stakeholder acceptance.

title: Unveiling the time value of carbon in underground infrastructure: A dynamic life-cycle assessment model for tunnel construction methods
abstract: While tunnel construction constitutes a significant component of carbon emissions in the transportation sector, comparative studies on the carbon footprints of different construction methods remain insufficient. More importantly, traditional life-cycle assessment models rely on static carbon accounting, fundamentally neglecting the time value of carbon emissions. To address this methodological gap, this study proposes a dynamic carbon emission flow model based on the analogy between carbon emissions and financial cash flows. The full life cycle of tunnel projects was divided into three stages: materialization, operation and maintenance, and final disposal. Five representative tunnel construction methods were systematically evaluated, including Tunnel Boring Machine, Cut-and-Cover, Pipe Jacking, Drill-and-Blast, and Shield Tunneling. Key dynamic parameters, such as the annual energy-consumption growth rate, were determined using an expert-consensus approach. The results indicate that the total dynamic carbon emission flows are approximately 23 to 25 times higher than the corresponding static carbon emission flows, demonstrating that the temporal distribution of emissions exerts a substantial influence on long-term environmental performance. Furthermore, after accounting for tunnel cross-sectional area and surrounding rock grade, the Tunnel Boring Machine method had the highest mean Integrated Carbon Emission Factor (4.87), whereas Shield Tunneling had the lowest (0.18). These findings highlight the importance of incorporating temporal carbon effects and engineering characteristics into tunnel carbon assessment. The proposed framework extends conventional life-cycle assessment by integrating temporal valuation and provides a more comprehensive basis for evaluating the long-term environmental impacts of alternative tunnel construction methods.

title: Phase transition and spatiotemporal distribution of CO2 hydrate influenced by coupled thermal and water heterogeneity
abstract: Artificial CO2 hydrate cap is considered a promising technology for coupling methane hydrate exploitation with long-term CO2 storage and climate mitigation. However, the dynamic formation and sealing performance remain poorly understood under coupled thermal conditions and spatially heterogeneous water distributions. In this study, low-field nuclear magnetic resonance (LF-NMR) was employed to visualize and quantify the spatiotemporal evolution of CO2 hydrate under varying thermal conditions and heterogeneous water distributions. Results show that hydrate formation is jointly governed by temperature and initial water distribution. Temperature primarily affects growth patterns and kinetics, while water distribution determines the location, morphology, and rate of hydrate formation. The hydrate growth pattern transitions from bidirectional (≤275.65 K) to unidirectional along the gas flow path (>275.65 K). Notably, stronger subcooling does not always enhance hydrate formation, as its thermodynamic advantage can be masked by heterogeneous water distribution, which alters gas-water contact and mass transfer pathways. Fractal analysis reveals a strong linear correlation (R2 ≈ 0.97) between fractal dimension and permeability, confirming that structural complexity effectively reflects sealing performance. Under optimized sealing conditions (274.65 K with non-uniform initial water distribution), permeability decreased to 0.00099 mD. The maximum CO2-to-hydrate conversion efficiency reached 94.53%, primarily controlled by initial water saturation. These findings provide quantitative guidance for optimizing hydrate-cap formation, improving CO2 storage efficiency and sealing performance, and reducing potential leakage risks, thereby supporting safer and more sustainable CO2 management.

title: Carbon footprint assessment of precast concrete products based on Environmental Product Declarations. Application to the case of Spain
abstract: The construction sector faces increasing regulatory pressure to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and to provide transparent, reliable and comparable environmental information for construction products. Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs), based on life cycle assessment (LCA), are progressively becoming mandatory instruments under the revised European Construction Products Regulation (EU) 2024/3110. However, empirical evidence on the internal consistency, variability and regulatory robustness of EPD datasets at national scale remains limited, particularly for industrialised construction systems such as precast concrete. This study provides the first comprehensive nationwide assessment of third-party verified EPDs for precast concrete products manufactured in Spain. It critically analyses a dataset of 69 EPDs, prepared in accordance with EN 15804 and EN 16757 standards and covering nine product categories, focusing on Global Warming Potential (GWP). The results are evaluated by life cycle stage to identify dominant emission sources, range of values and main factors of variability between company-specific and sectoral declarations. The results show that, while EPDs are an essential cornerstone for transparency and decarbonisation strategies in the precast concrete sector, their direct use for comparative decision-making and regulatory compliance is currently constrained by methodological heterogeneity. The study highlights the need for stricter harmonisation of modelling practices and interpretation standards to ensure that mandatory environmental disclosure effectively supports fair comparison, industrial decarbonisation and evidence-based policy implementation. These findings support the implementation of the revised EU Construction Products Regulation by highlighting the need for greater methodological harmonisation in EPD development.

title: Quantifying the environmental and social sustainability impact of material choice in metal additive manufacturing: A life cycle assessment approach
abstract: Compared to traditional subtractive manufacturing, metal additive manufacturing can achieve material and energy efficiency gains contributing to the sustainability of manufacturing in production systems and the achievement of several United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (e.g., UN-SDGs 3, 8, 10, 12, and 13). However, the sustainability benefits achievable through additive manufacturing depend strongly on material selection, raising the question of which candidate material offers the greatest benefits. As this question is poorly addressed in the available literature, this research compares ten alloy alternatives with a custom and easy-to-apply framework for environmental and social life cycle assessment only requiring physical characteristics and the chemical composition of the printing material. Laser powder bed fusion is chosen as the reference technology and Switzerland as the geographical reference. The generated quantitative and qualitative results, which are best interpreted as a mass-based comparative sustainability screening of candidate alloys under LPBF conditions, indicate that among the investigated alloys, AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy®, SS17-4 PH, SS316L, and M300 show good performance in both environmental and social sustainability dimensions. In contrast, In718, In625, CoCr and Ti6Al4V are less sustainable as feedstock materials. These findings, together with the sensitivity analyses, can inform scientific and industrial decision-making by introducing a sustainability perspective into currently mainly technically dominated decision processes in metal additive manufacturing, and provide a starting point for broader discussions in political and public realms. The research thereby supports more informed selection among viable feedstock materials, more sustainable production patterns, and progress toward international initiatives such as the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.

title: Effectiveness and trade-offs of leonardite and rock powder additives (zeolite, bentonite, lava rock dust, diabase, and basalt) for ammonia and greenhouse gas mitigation during cattle slurry storage
abstract: Ammonia (NH3) and greenhouse gas emissions from slurry storage represent major environmental challenges in livestock production. Additives such as humic substances and rock powders have been proposed as mitigation options. However, results regarding their effectiveness remain inconsistent, and their implications for nitrogen trade-offs between NH3 and nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions and total greenhouse gas emissions during slurry storage are poorly constrained. This study evaluated a humic substance (leonardite) and five rock powder additives (zeolite, bentonite, diabase, lava rock dust, and basalt) in controlled slurry storage. Additives were mixed with diluted untreated slurry at an application rate of 5% (w/w), and NH3 emissions were quantified by continuous acid trapping, while, N2O, methane (CH4), and carbon dioxide (CO2) were measured once daily during 10-min measurement periods, using the final 3 min for evaluation, over a 22-day storage period. Leonardite significantly reduced cumulative NH3 emissions by 32%, followed by zeolite with a 29% reduction, whereas other additives did not significantly affect NH3 emissions. However, ammonia reduction by leonardite was accompanied by a 20% increase in N2O emissions, suggesting potential nitrogen trade-offs, while zeolite reduced NH3 without increasing N2O emissions. Diabase and lava rock dust significantly reduced CO2 emissions by 20% and 14%, respectively. Across all treatments, CH4 contributed most to total greenhouse gas emissions expressed as CO2 equivalents and increased by up to 25–31% for some additives, offsetting potential environmental benefits from NH3, even after inclusion of indirect N2O emissions associated with NH3 volatilisation. Consequently, no treatment resulted in a significant reduction in total greenhouse gas emissions expressed as CO2 equivalents. Overall, mitigation effects during slurry storage were limited and additive specific. These findings highlight the need for integrated, multi-gas assessments to ensure robust environmental benefits.

title: Toward a unified modeling approach to Coupled Human–Natural Systems: Integrating Economic Input–Output models with MBSE-HFGT
abstract: Understanding sustainability challenges in the Anthropocene requires modeling tightly coupled human and natural systems (CHANS). While Economic Input–Output (EIO) models effectively map supply chains and resource flows, they are typically developed in disciplinary silos. This isolation makes it difficult to integrate economic models with energy, watershed, and climate systems, as they lack a common language. To address this gap, Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) and Systems Modeling Language (SysML) diagrams are used as a shared language to graphically represent both the structure of these diverse systems (form) and how they behave (function). These systems are then computationally simulated using Hetero-functional Graph Theory (HFGT). This provides a unified framework that preserves traditional economic mathematical rigor while enabling direct integration with other Anthropocene systems. This approach is validated using a static, single-period synthetic Rectangular Choice of Technology (RCOT) model. The MBSE-HFGT methodology reproduced the solution of the traditional RCOT model within the reported numerical precision, successfully optimizing factor utilization across six technological capabilities and five constraints. Consequently, for the first time, an EIO model is internalized within SysML diagrams and quantitatively simulated with HFGT, which lays the foundation for removing traditional barriers to coupling EIO models with other Anthropocene systems. Ultimately, this methodology can facilitate interdisciplinary knowledge co-production and offers a path toward modeling complex CHANS, to be demonstrated in future empirical applications.

title: Systematic bias in runoff and sediment attribution under hydroclimatic nonstationarity: Evidence from China's major river basins
abstract: Accurate attribution of runoff and sediment changes to climatic variability and human activities is important for understanding watershed responses to environmental change. However, conventional attribution methods can produce different estimates, and their biases remain poorly understood. Here, we use 543 high-quality paired samples from 22 representative catchments across China (1960-2024) to evaluate four widely used methods within a Similar Weather Condition (SWC) framework, including the double mass curve (DMC) and three Budyko-based elasticity methods. Conventional methods overestimated anthropogenic contributions to runoff changes at 54.55% of the stations, with a mean bias of +28.18%, but underestimated sediment contributions at 86.36% of the stations, with a mean bias of −3.81%. DMC showed the widest bias range among the four methods. Structural bias averaged 13.14% for runoff and −2.53% for sediment, whereas interaction effect bias varied substantially among stations. Climate–human interactions were mainly synergistic, with the interaction between aridity and human activity showing the strongest explanatory power for spatial variation in runoff and sediment bias (q = 0.967 and 0.989, respectively). The dominant controls differed among hydrologically similar catchment units. PLS-SEM revealed linked effects of climatic aridity and human activity, whereas interaction intensity was not significantly correlated with attribution bias. Thus, interaction intensity alone does not explain the magnitude of attribution bias. The SWC framework provides an observation-based benchmark for evaluating attribution bias in runoff and sediment studies across catchments with different hydro-environmental conditions.

title: Study on the spatiotemporal evolution laws of explosion in multi-scale pure H2/H2-blended natural gas pipelines leakage in open space
abstract: H2, as a clean and low-carbon energy source, plays an important role in promoting the energy transition and achieving the “dual carbon” goals. However, H2 or H2-blended natural gas can cause severe explosion accidents upon leakage. Due to the difficulty of conducting multi-scale explosion experiments in open space, relevant experimental data are scarce, a systematic understanding of the spatiotemporal evolution of such explosions remains difficult. This study lies in establishing a multi-scale experimental–numerical framework that quantitatively links hydrogen concentration, gas-cloud scale, and spatial confinement with the spatiotemporal evolution of explosion hazards. It shows that H2 increases the combustion rate and reaction intensity, leading to higher overpressure peaks. Enlarging the gas cloud further enhances the explosion intensity. Based on similarity criterion, it is pointed out that increasing the gas cloud volume nonlinearly amplifies the explosion load, demonstrating a pronounced scale effect. When the volume expands from 8 m3 to 144 m3, far-field overpressure and impulse increase by 51 and 94 times. Spatial confinement intensifies the explosion, as wall confinement causes shock-wave reflection and energy convergence, resulting in increased overpressure and wave speed near the wall. The proposed damage criterion and overpressure models are effective, with prediction errors within 20%. From an engineering perspective, the quantified explosion loads and hazard distances provide a basis for safety-distance determination, facility layout optimization, explosion protection, and emergency-response design for hydrogen infrastructure.

title: Lightweight cementitious composites incorporating accelerated-aged EPS insulation and microencapsulated phase change material for building envelopes
abstract: Expanded polystyrene (EPS) insulation retains low density and low thermal conductivity after long-term service, but its thermally aged condition has rarely been considered when EPS is used as an aggregate in cementitious materials. This study developed lightweight cementitious composites combining accelerated-aged EPS insulation aggregate, used as a controlled model of the thermally aged fraction of post-service EPS insulation, with n-octadecane-based microencapsulated phase change material (mPCM) for building-envelope applications. EPS boards were exposed to 70 °C for 180 days under an adapted EN 13166 heat-aging condition, crushed into 2–4 mm particles, and incorporated with mPCM as partial volumetric replacements for fine aggregate. EPS provided density reduction and passive insulation, whereas mPCM supplied latent-heat storage as a functionally distinct component. After aging, EPS thermal conductivity increased by only 1.73%. The lowest compressive strength, 6.60 MPa for E30mP30, remained above the 4.14 MPa minimum average strength specified by ASTM C129 for nonloadbearing concrete masonry units. DSC confirmed phase-change functionality, with E30mP30 exhibiting melting and crystallization enthalpies of 8.21 and 9.16 J/g. Its thermal conductivity was 0.5865 W/m·K, 52.1% lower than Plain. Additive-reference analyses indicated slightly sub-additive thermal conductivity and a slightly greater-than-additive heating delay, consistent with largely complementary contributions from EPS and mPCM. Across three repeated heating–cooling cycles, E30mP30 delayed the 25 °C heating crossing time by 5.6 ± 0.2 min relative to Plain, whereas mPCM prolonged the cooling passage through the 28–25 °C phase-change range by 5.8–7.0 min relative to Plain. Building simulations for Bogotá, Mexico City, and Los Angeles predicted total annual energy-demand reductions of up to 9.1%, corresponding to simulated operational CO2 reductions of approximately 9% under fixed grid-emission factors. These results provide a controlled laboratory basis for the reuse of thermally aged EPS insulation, which requires further validation using actual demolition-derived EPS and life-cycle assessment.

title: Does China’s pilot emissions trading scheme (ETS) policy affect the corporate core competence?
abstract: As a key market-based instrument for environmental regulation, the carbon emissions trading system (ETS) holds the potential to reshape corporate development trajectories, but its firm-level effects remain debated. This study examines the impact of China's pilot ETS policy on corporate core competence. Employing factor analysis, this study constructs a comprehensive evaluation model for corporate core competence, utilizing it to calculate firms' overall core competence scores as well as their scores across various principal component factors. Treating the pilot ETS as a quasi-natural experiment, a difference-in-differences model was constructed to assess its effects on covered firms. The results show that the ETS policy is significantly negatively associated with corporate core competence, profitability, financial stability, and operational efficiency in pilot areas, with financial stability being the least affected. The negative effects also display significant industry heterogeneity. The adverse effects are particularly pronounced in the chemical, building materials, and electric power sectors, whereas no significant impact is observed within the steel industry. Overall, the findings indicate that the pilot ETS generates short-term adjustment pressure on regulated firms and the resulting consequences vary significantly across different industries.

title: Comprehensive analysis of fiber release from fleece knitted fabrics during repeated maintenance and mechanical abrasion
abstract: Fiber release from textile products has become an important environmental concern because fibers are continuously emitted throughout the service life of textiles and may contribute to environmental contamination. Although numerous studies have investigated fiber release during laundering, the combined effects of repeated washing, tumble drying, and mechanical abrasion on the degradation and fiber-release behavior of fleece knitted fabrics remain insufficiently understood. This study comprehensively evaluated three fleece knitted fabrics differing in fiber composition and morphology: cotton staple fibers, virgin polyester (PES) multifilament fibers, and recycled PES multifilament fibers. Fiber release during repeated washing, tumble drying, and mechanical abrasion was quantified gravimetrically. Structural changes were characterized using image analysis based on the surface cover factor (CF), fiber-length distribution analysis, and air-permeability measurements. Mechanical abrasion was evaluated using a modified laboratory procedure designed to provide controlled and accelerated mechanical loading for comparative assessment of fiber release. Fiber release during washing and tumble drying exhibited a characteristic exponential decline during the initial maintenance cycles and stabilized after approximately six to eight cycles, indicating the progressive removal of loosely anchored surface fibers. In contrast, fiber release increased continuously with increasing abrasion time, demonstrating that mechanical wear is governed by a different degradation mechanism. The cotton fleece knitted fabric exhibited the largest fiber release during the initial maintenance cycles, while differences among the investigated materials depended on the type of mechanical loading and the evaluated structural parameter. Compared with the investigated virgin PES fabric, the recycled PES fabric exhibited higher air permeability and greater variability in several measured fiber-release and structural parameters. These differences reflect the combined effects of fiber characteristics and fabric structure, which could not be independently separated in the commercial materials investigated. A strong correlation between the surface cover factor and the amount of released fibers confirmed that progressive changes in surface morphology are closely associated with fiber detachment. The results demonstrate that fiber release is governed not only by fiber composition but also by the type of mechanical loading acting throughout the textile service life. The combined evaluation of surface morphology, fiber-length distributions, and air permeability provides a comprehensive understanding of the degradation processes controlling fiber release and offers valuable guidance for the development of textile materials with improved durability and reduced fiber emissions.

title: Towards post-growth policymaking: Barriers and enablers for wellbeing economy and Doughnut economics initiatives
abstract: Providing wellbeing for all while safeguarding planetary boundaries may require governments to pursue post-growth policies. An important question is the extent to which government-led post-growth initiatives can be transformative within the existing institutional context. Initial empirical studies have highlighted some of the limitations these initiatives currently face, but a broader empirical assessment of the underlying barriers and enablers across institutional contexts is still lacking. To address this gap, we examine wellbeing economy and Doughnut economics government initiatives across governance scales in Europe, New Zealand, and Canada. To identify barriers and enablers as well as priorities for future action, we develop and apply a framework that captures systemic and political dimensions to analyze the data. Overall, our results suggest that the overarching economic growth paradigm severely limits the initiatives’ scope of action. Important enablers of existing initiatives in our study include crises, the political agency of key individuals, and high-level political support. Civil servants who promote growth-critical perspectives often face tensions: they need to appeal to broad stakeholder groups while avoiding co-optation. To create the political and organizational conditions for transformative policy change we suggest focusing on two areas: fostering a critical consciousness of growth hegemony in society, and institutionally embedding post-growth-aligned political priorities whenever there are political windows of opportunity. Strengthening government-led post-growth initiatives will also require stronger engagement with — and pressure from — civil society.

title: Geological prescreen maps for pressure and plume management in CO2 storage well-layout design: A case study of the Shenhua CCS project
abstract: Scaling carbon capture and storage (CCS) in deep saline aquifers requires well layouts that coordinate injection, pressure management, and mobile-CO2 migration within heterogeneous reservoirs. We develop a geological-prescreening-driven surrogate-assisted workflow that embeds plan-view and well-column descriptors of transmissive organization, vertical architecture, and pressure safety into multi-objective well-layout search. Application to the field-scale Shenhua CCS model shows three distinct response drivers within the evaluated layout ensemble. The pressure-peak magnitude is associated primarily with the transmissive capacity reached by brine producers, the projected mobile-CO2 footprint with vertical stacking in the injection interval, and spatial pressure heterogeneity with the geometric match between injection sources and production sinks. XGBoost surrogates and NSGA-III support the identification of these geological associations while avoiding repeated full-physics evaluations during the search, and the selected layouts are subsequently verified with the simulator. The resulting framework links three-dimensional geological characterization to interpretable pressure, plume, and well-layout decisions for heterogeneous saline-aquifer storage.

title: Reconciling thermal storage and fire safety in biomass-derived phase change composites via a synergistic carbon aerogel/MPP framework
abstract: Organic phase change materials (PCMs) hold immense promise for thermal energy storage but are plagued by intrinsic flammability and leakage risks. To reconcile the conflict between high energy density and fire safety, this study develops a novel shape-stabilized composite PCM by confining n-octadecane within a biomass-derived carbon aerogel (CA) framework, synergistically reinforced with melamine pyrophosphate (MPP) and a flame-retardant adhesive (FRA). The CA support, synthesized via a facile low-temperature (300 °C) molten salt strategy, provides a mesoporous network that effectively prevents leakage and slightly improves thermal conductivity. Crucially, the introduction of MPP and FRA creates a ternary synergistic flame-retardant system, which forms a “gas-solid” synergistic flame-retardant network, substantiated by direct TG-FTIR evidence, to block heat transfer and oxygen diffusion. The optimized composite (PCMs-7) delivers a high enthalpy of 77.7 J/g, a significant reduction in peak heat release rate (from 442 to 24 kW/m2), and a UL-94 V-0 rating with a Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) of 26.3%. Furthermore, the composite exhibits favorable preliminary thermal reliability over 600 cycles, retaining 93.7% of its initial enthalpy. This work demonstrates a viable approach for designing fire-safe, leakage-proof, and durable thermal energy storage materials for advanced applications.

title: An activity-based framework for assessing impacts of industrial symbiosis as a pathway to industrial decarbonisation
abstract: Meeting the emissions reduction targets of the Paris Agreement requires manufacturing industries to move beyond incremental efficiency measures toward systemic change. Industrial symbiosis (IS) — the deliberate exchange of industrial waste streams and by-products between companies — represents a credible yet largely underutilised decarbonisation pathway capable of delivering substantial carbon reductions. Despite growing regulatory pressure and long-term net-zero commitments, IS remains largely absent from corporate decarbonisation strategies, in part because existing IS tools were not designed to translate a candidate IS exchange into a comprehensive assessment that supports a business case to decarbonise. This study addresses that barrier by proposing the Activity-Based Industrial Symbiosis Framework (AISF), a systematic methodology that decomposes bilateral IS exchanges into their constituent engineering activities, quantifies the carbon impact of each activity through a carbon ledger across different scenarios of synergy implications, and qualitatively maps the accompanying environmental, economic and social consequences for each activity and stakeholder. Applied to an operational food and beverage sector IS case study under baseline and progressive integration scenarios, the framework demonstrates that IS in this case study delivers substantial reductions in carbon intensity per unit of product, with the dominant emission source shifting structurally from primary production to logistics as integration deepens. Sensitivity analysis of the case indicates that the environmental benefit is robust within the modelled range of transport distance and solids content. This study demonstrates that AISF provides corporate sustainability decision-makers, policymakers and IS facilitators with a structured, activity-resolved tool. This framework has the potential to transfer to other exchanges for identifying and quantifying IS as a measurable contribution to industrial decarbonisation.

title: Drivers of overall satisfaction with urban street blocks: A SHAP-based analysis of winter–summer differences
abstract: Overall satisfaction with urban street blocks is not a linear response to any single environmental attribute but an integrative appraisal shaped by microclimate, built environment, thermal perceptions, psychological perceptions, and personal features. However, winter–summer differences, class-specific asymmetries, and cross-domain interactions remain insufficiently understood. Synchronous microclimatic measurements and questionnaire surveys were conducted at six sites across three representative street blocks in Hefei, China, yielding 1964 valid responses (1140 in winter and 824 in summer). A theory-informed feature engineering pipeline reduced 55 candidate predictors to 26, and nine machine learning classifiers were systematically benchmarked. The best-performing Extra Trees models for the seasonal datasets were subsequently interpreted using Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to quantify global importance, class-specific contributions, and feature interactions. Extra Trees achieved micro-AUC of 0.985 in winter and 0.995 in summer. Predictive attribution was dominated by psychological and perceptual variables rather than objective microclimatic parameters. Stress relief ranked first in winter (19.2%), whereas visual satisfaction dominated summer (17.6%); safety and perceived wind speed also became more prominent in summer. Feature contributions were asymmetric across dissatisfied, neutral, and satisfied classes: visual satisfaction and preference degree contributed primarily to predictions of satisfaction, whereas low perceived safety and extreme thermal sensation were more closely associated with dissatisfaction. Moreover, interactions between perceived paving quality and key thermal parameters reversed across seasons, indicating that climatic context conditions the perceived value of design attributes. These findings advance an interpretable, context-sensitive framework linking physical exposure, multisensory and thermal appraisal, psychological response, and overall evaluation, thereby providing quantitative evidence for human-centered, seasonally adaptive street block renewal.

title: Integrated climate assessment of multifunctional grassland biorefinery: effects of co-product use and allocation methods
abstract: Exploring climate-friendly valorization of locally available biomass is important for advancing the circular bioeconomy. Multi-species grasslands provide benefits, including carbon sequestration, reduced nitrogen losses, and biodiversity support, and are traditionally used as ruminant feed. Alternatively, grassland biomass can be processed in a biorefinery to produce leaf protein concentrate (LPC) for monogastric feed, together with fiber press cake and brown juice as co-products. The fiber press cake can be used for ruminant feed, biogas production, or packaging materials, while brown juice can be used for biogas production or field application. Another valorization pathway is the direct use of grassland biomass for biogas production through anaerobic digestion, with digestate generated as a co-product that can be applied to agricultural fields. To assess the climate impacts of multi-species grassland production and subsequent valorization pathways, life cycle assessment (LCA) was applied using two approaches for handling multifunctionality: economic allocation and system expansion by substitution. The analysis was conducted in three steps. First, climate impacts of biomass production up to the farm gate were assessed for three grassland mixtures designed for protein production (Protein), biodiversity enhancement (Pollinator), and bioenergy production (Energy), under two harvesting regimes (two and four cuts per year). Second, the climate impact of LPC production at the biorefinery gate was assessed using the four-cut Protein mixture. Six co-product-use configurations were evaluated under both economic allocation and system expansion by substitution, resulting in 12 modelled scenarios, in addition to a baseline in which all impacts were assigned to LPC. Third, the Energy mixture under both two- and four-cut regimes was assessed for biogas production. LPC and biogas-derived methane were benchmarked against soybean-based feeds and fossil methane, respectively. The farm-gate GWP of grassland biomass ranged from 55 to 105 kg CO2-eq per ton of grass dry matter, mainly influenced by N2O emissions, diesel use, and soil carbon changes. The GWP of LPC ranged from −115 to 1383 kg CO2-eq per ton of LPC dry matter under system expansion and from 938 to 1040 kg CO2-eq per ton of LPC dry matter under economic allocation. On a crude protein-equivalent basis, LPC showed comparable or lower GWP than soybean-based feeds, while biogas-derived methane produced from the Energy mixture showed a 61-91% lower GWP than fossil methane on an energy-equivalent basis. Overall, the results highlight the importance of co-product use and multifunctionality handling in determining the climate performance of grassland biorefinery pathways.

title: The impacts of R&D induced technological change supported by China's Emissions Trading Scheme revenues
abstract: Despite the potential of China's carbon Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) revenues, their usage and allocation remain underexplored. Being used to support sectoral R&D induced technological change (ITC) could be an ideal investment for such carbon revenue. This study integrates an ITC component into a multi-regional dynamic computable general equilibrium (ITC-CGE) model to assess the socioeconomic and environmental impacts of reallocating ETS revenues to sectoral R&D subsidies, with the core objective of comparing 24 predefined ETS revenue-recycling scenarios and identifying preferred scenarios for individual provinces under explicitly stated economic and environmental evaluation criteria. The results show that while using ETS revenues for R&D subsidies can result in GDP and welfare losses, the technological advancements reduce energy consumption and optimize structural efficiencies, lowering overall social abatement costs. Targeted subsidies, particularly in high-carbon-intensity regions, minimize welfare loss. When directed at the power sector, R&D subsidies from ETS revenues further reduce GDP losses, increase power sector profits, and enhance energy consumption and generation efficiencies. To maximize CO2 reduction cost-effectiveness, high-carbon-intensity provinces (e.g., Anhui, Shanxi) should allocate ETS revenues across all high-emission sectors, while low-carbon-intensity provinces (e.g., Fujian, Jiangsu) should focus on R&D in green sectors such as renewable energy. This study provides novel insights into optimizing ETS revenue strategies, advocating for differentiated provincial and sectoral approaches to stimulate technological innovation.

title: Unraveling the coordination between multi-dimensional urbanization and resource and environment carrying capacity in China: Aggregation patterns, influencing mechanisms and policy implications
abstract: The coordination between multi-dimensional urbanization (MUR) and resource and environment carrying capacity (RECC) is crucial for China’s sustainable development. Current research mainly focuses on evaluating the coupling coordination degree (CCD) between MUR and RECC at the city and watershed scales. However, comprehensive investigations into the spatial clustering patterns of CCD evolution and their underlying influencing mechanisms at the national scale remain scarce. To address the research gap, this study employed the CCD model, spatial autocorrelation analysis, boosted regression tree model, and spatial Durbin model to systematically explore the evolution trends, spatial clustering characteristics, and influencing mechanisms of the CCD between MUR and RECC in China. The results show that from 2003 to 2022, the average CCD value across 31 Chinese provinces increased from 0.43 to 0.64, with a growth rate of 48.84%. Spatially, the CCD exhibited significant regional heterogeneity, with an overall spatial distribution ranking of East China > Central China > North China > South China > Southwest China > Northeast China > Northwest China. At the provincial level, pronounced spatial clustering patterns emerge, characterized by High-High clustering predominantly in the eastern regions and Low-Low clustering in the western regions. Notably, urbanization has become the primary influencing factor for CCD variations across China, with social urbanization and economic urbanization exerting the strongest influence. Based on the distinct development characteristics of different regions, this study proposed three targeted strategies: synergistic development strategy, resource advantage transformation strategy, and economic enhancement strategy. These findings provide both theoretical foundations and technical guidance for advancing sustainable regional development.

title: Sustainable periodic delivery of fresh food: Integrating energy consumption, driver fairness and customer fairness
abstract: In fresh food delivery, high transportation energy consumption, driver workload imbalances, and customer unfairness pose critical challenges to sustainable operations. To jointly optimize environmental and social sustainability objectives, this study proposes a fairness-aware periodic green vehicle routing problem (FA-PGVRP). An optimization model is developed that simultaneously considers transportation energy consumption, driver fairness, and customer fairness. To address this problem, a fairness-aware hybrid genetic algorithm (FA-HGA) is proposed by embedding driver-fairness and customer-fairness search operators into the genetic framework, to facilitate fairness-guided search and mitigate the limitations of post-decoding solution evaluation. Experiments based on a real-world case in Shehong City, China, and benchmark instances of varying scales demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Compared with the existing strategy (ES) and the energy-focused strategy (EFS), the proposed energy consumption and fairness-aware strategy (EC-FAS) reduces driver unfairness and customer unfairness by approximately 50% while incurring only a marginal increase in transportation energy consumption. Furthermore, trade-off analyses reveal significant conflicts between energy consumption and fairness objectives, whereas driver fairness and customer fairness exhibit weak interactions. Substantial improvements in both fairness dimensions can be achieved with only about a 10% increase in energy consumption, indicating a manageable trade-off between environmental and social sustainability objectives. These findings provide quantitative decision support for sustainable periodic fresh food delivery.

title: Grain-inspired cellulose-based adsorption-filtration platform for ultrafast cobalt capture and safe volumetric reduction from nuclear wastewater
abstract: Radioactive cobalt in nuclear power plant wastewater demands rapid removal and safe disposal, yet existing adsorbents are kinetically slow and generate persistent secondary waste. Here, inspired by the metal-chelating function of phytic acid in cereal grains, we graft phytic acid onto bamboo cellulose fibers via a one-step, solvent-free solid-phase esterification to create a bioinspired adsorption membrane (PA@BCM) with a disordered, loosely stacked microstructure that enables rapid mass transport. Integrated into an adsorption-filtration process instead of single adsorption, PA@BCM removes 99.33% of radioactive cobalt from 2.1 L of simulated wastewater within just 5 min at pilot scale with a parallel configuration, drastically outperforming the commercial AmberLite™ IRN77 resin that requires hours to reach equilibrium. Unlike conventional resins that demand cementation of the entire spent adsorbent for storage, the all-biomass PA@BCM could be decomposed under inert atmosphere to reduce 80.06% of the spent adsorbent volume, which corresponds to a 72.76% reduction in long-term waste storage space after cementation. Beyond cobalt, PA@BCM also shows high removal efficiencies toward other radionuclides (e.g., Sr2+, Ce3+) and heavy metals (e.g., Cu2+, Pb2+). Our work establishes a scalable, bio-based platform that transforms radioactive wastewater treatment from a linear adsorb-then-solidify process into an integrated, waste-minimizing solution.

title: Adoption dynamics of integrated home renovation pathways by homeowner associations: A multi-case study from the Netherlands
abstract: The uptake of deep energy renovations in European condominiums remains limited, despite the emergence of innovative Integrated Home Renovation Services (IHRS) that aim to reduce recognized barriers. Despite introducing new renovation possibilities, the extent to which these services are adopted is shaped by homeowners' views of their relevance, feasibility, and associated risks. The paper examines homeowners’ experiences with market-driven renovation pathways and highlights the key conditions required to enable their wider adoption. This study aims to answer the question: How are market-driven renovation pathways perceived and adopted by homeowner associations, and how do different renovation pathways shape these adoption dynamics? The study draws on four Dutch case studies representing different pathways for energy renovation. These include two integrated renovation concepts built around a living-cost-neutral approach, a phased pathway combining completed and planned renovation measures, and a financing strategy based on densification through rooftop extensions. Empirical material was gathered through semi-structured interviews with private IHRS providers and homeowners, together with document review and expert workshops. Homeowners differed in how they experienced financial risks, governance issues, trust, and uncertainty during the process. The cases showed that progress was often slowed by the need for collective agreement, long and demanding processes, and a lack of alignment between institutions. Based on these findings, the study identifies implications for IHRS service and business-model design and for policy support, with lessons for adapting market-driven renovation pathways to other European condominium contexts.

title: Structural transfer learning for early-phase carbon price prediction: A case study from the EU ETS to the Korean ETS
abstract: Accurate carbon price forecasting is essential to maintaining market stability, yet emerging emissions trading systems (ETSs) are severely constrained by data scarcity. Since conventional forecasting models typically rely on autoregressive price lags and large sets of observations, these models are inappropriate for emerging markets that lack historical data. To overcome this, this study proposes a cross-market transfer learning (TL) framework based on a strict structural-only feature constraint, in which input features are restricted to exogenous international energy prices, economic policy indicators, and ETS mechanism design parameters. The TL framework consists of a training process where the CatBoost model learns the foundational market behavior from the mature EU ETS as the source domain. The structural knowledge of this pre-trained model is then transferred and fine-tuned to the Korean ETS target domain, utilizing only early-phase data to simulate a data-scarce condition. Additionally, a progressive chronological expanding window strategy is employed to ensure robust forecasting evaluation without look-ahead bias. The predictive model achieves a test R2 of 0.941, demonstrating strong predictive performance compared to alternative machine learning and baseline models. Upon transfer, the fine-tuned model demonstrates promising predictive performance under data-scarce conditions. Fine-tuning reduces forecast errors relative to direct transfer even with only one quarter of target-market data, although at that stage the improvement is not yet statistically significant; significance emerges as target-market observations accumulate, within about a year in our setting. Beyond predictive performance, SHAP analysis shows that ETS mechanism parameters, particularly the allowance cap, free allocation ratio, and sectoral market concentration, are among the most significant drivers of carbon price, alongside energy prices. Overall, this study provides a framework for structural cross-market knowledge transfer under data-scarce conditions and predictive insights that may equip policymakers and market participants with data-driven information to support decision-making and the development of emerging carbon markets.

title: Modular labor division and targeted metabolic regulation driven by high-pressure carbon dioxide pretreatment for enhancing food waste acidogenic fermentation
abstract: High-pressure carbon dioxide (HPCD) pretreatment is a promising strategy for enhancing the acidogenic fermentation (AF) of food waste. However, balancing physical macromolecule disruption with biological microbial inactivation has become a critical challenge. In this study, the AF of a lipid- and protein-rich model substrate pretreated with varying HPCD pressures (1 - 4 MPa) was investigated. The results showed that among the evaluated HPCD pressures, a 2 MPa pretreatment achieved optimal yields of volatile fatty acids (VFAs), specifically directing metabolic flux toward acetate. Additionally, the pretreatment with 2 MPa achieved an optimal balance between endogenous enzymatic hydrolysis and targeted indigenous microbiota inactivation. This stress-resistant micro-environment facilitated exogenous sludge microbe colonization and triggered targeted metabolic regulation, facilitating enhanced acetyl-CoA accumulation, thereby increasing the availability of a key metabolic precursor for VFA generation. Furthermore, this microenvironment promoted the formation of a modular network in which Escherichia-Shigella and Citrobacter acted as primary fermenters, rapidly degrading substrates to supply core precursors for terminal acetate synthesis by Lawsonella and Clostridium_sensu_stricto_3. This study provides a promising strategy for optimizing resource recovery from complex biomass.

title: Partial circularity: Waste burden and recovery pathways in OECD countries
abstract: Circular economy monitoring increasingly recognizes that recycling and recovery do not by themselves demonstrate lower material pressure. Less developed is a comparative framework for diagnosing national waste systems in which downstream treatment improves without a corresponding reduction in the waste entering municipal systems. Partial circularity is developed as a diagnostic concept for this mismatch and is operationalized through national waste regimes. A merged OECD country-year dataset covering 38 countries from 2015 to 2023 is used to distinguish municipal waste generation per person (waste burden) from treatment pathways. Four 2022 regimes are derived by crossing waste generation with broad recovery, and country-year models examine associations with consumption, material throughput, fiscal, spatial, and institutional conditions. Median municipal waste generation rose from 456.5 kg per person in 2015 to 497.2 kg in 2023, while broad recovery rose from 66.7% to 83.0% and landfill dependence declined. Several high-recovery systems nevertheless remained highly waste intensive. Multicollinearity diagnostics and robustness checks indicate that the most stable statistical pattern is the association between consumption and waste burden, while pathway outcomes also vary with material, spatial, and institutional conditions. Partial circularity complements existing indicator critiques by identifying and comparing cases in which downstream progress outpaces upstream burden reduction without proposing a causal theory of transition.

title: ESG competencies as enablers of sustainable and clean transitions in project-based work: An importance-performance analysis
abstract: Sustainable and clean transitions hinge on a capability that policy and corporate ESG commitments routinely overlook: the competencies of the project professionals who must actually deliver them. ESG principles are widely promoted, yet whether they translate into practice depends on project managers' ability to embed sustainability into planning, governance, and execution - and evidence on where these competencies fall short remains scarce. This study applies Importance-Performance Analysis (IPA) to a large-scale survey of project professionals across diverse organizational contexts, mapping the gap between what ESG competencies practitioners judge important and what they report delivering, across Environmental, Social, and Governance dimensions and across governance roles, organizational size, and experience. The results are unambiguous: gaps appear consistently across all three ESG dimensions, showing that implementation stalls on capability, not awareness. Environmental competencies carry the largest average gap; Governance is the most strategically urgent dimension - rated most important overall, containing the single largest competency gap, and concentrating the most competencies where high importance meets serious underperformance. Deficits cluster predictably: Environmental in green technology, life-cycle assessment, and innovation; Governance in ESG reporting, regulatory awareness, and training; Social in inclusivity, community impact, and human rights due diligence. Capability is structurally patterned - stronger among programme and portfolio managers, weaker in smaller organizations - pointing to where intervention should target first. By treating ESG as a measurable system of project-level competencies and using IPA to diagnose exactly where it breaks down, this study gives sustainable project management and cleaner production research a concrete, prioritized roadmap for closing the gap between ambition and delivery.

title: Bio-pitch and coal-tar pitch mixture as a binder in carbon anodes for aluminium electrolysis
abstract: The aluminium electrolysis process uses pre-baked carbon anodes as electricity conductors. Anode baking and consumption in the electrolysis cell generate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. A possible strategy to reduce these emissions is to partially substitute fossil-based coal-tar pitch (CTP) with biomass-sourced bio-pitch (BP) in anode formulation. CTP also releases harmful polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) when it is baked. In the current work, we attempted to mix BP and CTP at the concentration of CTP between 10 wt% and 90 wt% to produce alternative binders with acceptable properties. The coking value, softening point, viscosity, and surface functional groups of the mixtures were determined. According to the findings, mixing BP and CTP with increasing concentration of CTP increased the coking value of the mixtures of BP and CTP while maintaining favorable rheological properties. A mixture binder containing 45 wt% CTP was further studied in terms of its microstructure, wettability to coke, and mass loss behavior. The crystallinity and the specific surface area of the baked mixture binder were also determined. Lab-scale anodes made from the new mixture binder showed a higher baked apparent density, a lower electrical resistivity, and lower air reactivity compared to BP-based anodes. The new binder exhibited improved performance in laboratory-scale anodes, and life-cycle assessment of anode production revealed potential climate change impact reductions of 11 % compared to CTP binder. This approach can provide guidance to transition from CTP-based anodes to BP-based anodes without compromising the properties and performance of the former, while reducing GHG emissions and PAH emissions.

title: Bioinspired glycolipids as dust mitigation agents for mining environments
abstract: Airborne particulate matter (PM), including dust produced by natural and anthropogenic sources, continues to pose serious human and environmental health risks. While various dust suppression materials exist, innovations in sustainable and biodegradable alternatives remain a priority, particularly those that can reduce reliance on water-intensive or persistent chemical suppressants in industrial settings. Here, we present a systematic evaluation of sixteen bioinspired glycolipids as dust suppressants for mine tailings, a fine-grained mineral waste generated during ore processing. The glycolipids were designed with controlled variations in sugar headgroup type (e.g., xylose vs. rhamnose) and number (e.g., mono- vs. disaccharide), as well as lipid tail length (C10-C18) and number (single vs. double tail), facilitating targeted comparisons of molecular features and dust reduction capabilities. Structure-property-performance analyses indicate that lipid tail characteristics and molecular amphiphilicity considerably affect PM reduction efficacy. Single head single tail glycolipids exhibited enhanced performance with increasing tail length, while double tail variants consistently outperformed their single tail analogues, likely reflecting improved amphiphilic balance and interfacial behavior. Molecular amphiphilicity, quantified via calculated octanol-water partition coefficients (logP), displayed an optimal range of 6.5-11.5 associated with enhanced dust suppression among the tested glycolipids. In simulated wind erosion tests, fifteen glycolipids outperformed water, the most widely used suppressant, and eight achieved >90% PM reduction relative to water-treated controls. These results highlight the potential of sustainably produced glycolipids to support cleaner production practices in the mining sector by enabling effective dust mitigation for mine tailings and reducing environmental burdens.

title: From equity to sustainability: The shifting dynamics of common prosperity in China
abstract: Since the reform and opening-up, China has maintained sustained and stable economic growth, accompanied by a series of imbalanced development challenges. How to achieve common prosperity has thus become a critical issue to be addressed urgently. To explore the core influencing factors and evolutionary laws of common prosperity, this study constructs a system-dynamics model for common prosperity grounded in system theory and the information dynamic feedback theory, which covers four core subsystems: economic growth, income distribution, public services, and ecological environment. Multi-dimensional validations are performed on the model, including historical-data fitting test, robustness test, sensitivity analysis and extreme-scenario test. The results reveal that the four pathways — economic growth, income distribution, public services and ecological environment — exert significant positive driving effects on common prosperity. Furthermore, core driving factors present a phased transition feature, shifting gradually from “income distribution” toward “ecological environment”, reflecting a dynamic evolutionary trend from “equity-orientation” to “sustainable development”. From a systemic perspective, this paper investigates the dynamic evolution of core drivers behind China's common prosperity. By characterizing pathway feedbacks and evolutionary trends via system dynamics, it improves the explanatory and practical capacity of social-science research for complex real-world issues. Practically, it provides a targeted policy-making framework for promoting common prosperity in a phased manner.

title: Trade-based assessment of value-chain vulnerability in green hydrogen production
abstract: Understanding the vulnerability of emerging energy systems is essential for ensuring a resilient transition towards low‑carbon technologies. This study develops a trade‑based vulnerability framework to quantify systemic vulnerability in clean energy value‑chain. The methodology integrates three trade‑related indicators at the product level - revealed comparative advantage, market concentration, and net trade position - to capture competitiveness, supplier concentration, and import dependence, respectively. Product‑level risk scores are aggregated into value‑chain stages using economically grounded weights. A propagation parameter is then introduced to transmit upstream risks to downstream activities, generating a system-level vulnerability index that accounts for interdependencies across the chain. The framework is applied to the global green hydrogen value chain, covering critical raw materials, renewable energy technologies, electrolysers, and storage components. The results identify critical raw materials and solar photovoltaic technologies as the principal sources of structural vulnerability, while electrolysers and storage technologies exhibit comparatively lower exposure. Germany and China consistently exhibit the lowest levels of trade-based structural vulnerability, declining by 1.3% and 4.6%, respectively, between 2021 and 2024. Comparison with IEA green hydrogen production capacity rankings showed a moderate positive association (Spearman's ρ = 0.441 and p-value 0.0519). Overall, the study provides a transparent and operational framework for evaluating the vulnerability of strategic clean energy supply chains.

title: Expanding bio-plastics manufacturing in USA to replace conventional plastics: An environmentally extended input–output analysis with technology adoption and new bio-plastic sector
abstract: The demand for bioplastics is increasing because of advances in production technologies and growing interest in environmentally sustainable materials. Although bioplastics account for about 0.5% of the approximately 431 million metric tons of plastics produced annually, their market share is expected to increase over the next decade. However, the economy-wide implications of introducing bioplastics at scale remain inadequately studied. This study integrates an environmentally extended input–output model with process modeling to evaluate the economic and greenhouse gas implications of substituting conventional plastic packaging with polylactic acid (PLA) in the United States. Capital requirements and supply-chain effects were estimated for substitution levels of 10%, 25%, 50%, and 100% using process-based PLA facility cost data. A new bioplastics sector was incorporated into the existing economic model to evaluate the impacts of a $1 million demand for bioplastics and packaging production under each substitution scenario. Capital investment increases from about $6 billion for 10% substitution to about $52 billion for full substitution. These investments would generate total supply-chain economic impacts of about $9.9 billion and $87 billion, respectively. For a $1 million bioplastics demand, greenhouse gas emissions ranged from 577 to 681 metric tons of CO2 equivalent, compared with 889 metric tons for conventional plastics. Packaging-related emissions also declined from 296 metric tons of CO2 equivalent at 10% substitution to 267 metric tons at full substitution. These findings show that bioplastics can reduce supply-chain greenhouse gas emissions and support the decarbonization of packaging systems despite requiring substantial capital investment.

title: Life cycle assessment-guided cleaner production of amikacin: Sustainability analysis among eight synthesis routes
abstract: Pharmaceutical manufacturing can impose substantial environmental burdens because active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) synthesis often requires energy intensive operations, large solvent inputs, and multi-step protection, reaction, and purification procedures. This study applied an early-stage, cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment to compare eight reported amikacin synthesis routes on a mass-based functional unit of 1 g amikacin. Route-specific inventories reconstructed from literature and patent procedures were modeled as separate foreground systems in Activity Browser, linked to ecoinvent 3.9.1 cut-off and biosphere3, and characterized with ReCiPe 2016 across 14 midpoint categories and three endpoint areas. Uncertainty was examined using a 1000-iteration Monte Carlo analysis and S-proxy sensitivity cases with safety factors of 1, 2, and 4. The eight routes showed marked differences in environmental performance. AMK-5 had the lowest within-study aggregated midpoint index (0.41), approximately 94.9% lower than AMK-1 (8.11), which had the highest index. Electricity use was a dominant hotspot across multiple impact categories, while solvent use, protecting-group chemistry, and purification requirements created route specific burdens. Notably, solvent recovery alone increased several impacts under the modeled baseline electricity background because additional recovery energy offset part of the avoided solvent-production burden; coupling recovery with lower-impact electricity supply reversed this trade-off and improved environmental performance. Under the modeled conditions, the results highlight the importance of considering synthesis route design, electricity supply, and solvent management together. Their relevance to industrial production, as well as the applicability of the proposed workflow to other semisynthetic aminoglycosides, requires further validation.

title: Coordinating without convergence: How wave energy firms manage fragmented technical knowledge
abstract: Wave energy is the largest marine energy resource globally. Yet after 50 years of development, no technology has achieved commercial-scale deployment. In Ireland alone, the theoretical potential could reach 31.1 GW, but commercial wave projects have yet to be deployed in Irish waters. Unlike solar photovoltaics or offshore wind, which converged around dominant designs and enabled economies of scale, wave energy remains characterised by significant technological diversity across fundamentally different device concepts. This research explores how Irish wave energy firms coordinate knowledge to advance product architectures when technological consensus remains absent and market pull is weak. Through qualitative analysis of 12 Irish SMEs, we reveal that recognising viable architectural innovations depends on inter-organisational coordination mechanisms that enable multi-actor, cross-sectoral collective sensemaking rather than individual firms' capabilities alone. Specifically, we identify technical standards as a knowledge codification mechanism subject to a commercialisation ‘catch-22’: firms need deployment to validate designs, but cannot deploy without standards, yet standards cannot emerge without consensus on core architectural principles. Our findings demonstrate that orchestrating product architecture knowledge becomes a collective enterprise when distributed across the wave energy ecosystem, extending dominant design theory from firm-centric to system-level analysis. We explain how this transition risks stalling despite its technical feasibility.

title: Towards cleaner ethanol biomanufacturing: ORP-assisted soft sensing and multi-horizon forecasting in very-high-gravity fermentation
abstract: Very-high-gravity (VHG) ethanol fermentation can increase ethanol titer and reduce downstream demand, but deviations are difficult to detect from delayed offline assays. We developed a two-stage framework that reconciles sparse high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) measurements with dense oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) records, estimates current metabolic rates (ORP-State-Now, ORPSN), and forecasts future trajectories (ORP-State-Cast, ORPSC). Models were evaluated by six-fold leave-batch-out cross-validation in which complete test batches were excluded from model fitting, validation, and scaling. At 127 original HPLC sampling points per analyte, integrated ORPSN predictions achieved R2 values of 0.976 for ethanol and 0.991 for glucose, with root-mean-square errors of 6.76 and 9.78 g L−1. A three-seed ablation using the same RNN architecture showed that the ORP-core operational input bundle substantially outperformed a strict time-only baseline. ORPSC retained useful accuracy up to 8 h, but it does not model future manipulated variables and is an early-warning forecaster rather than a controller. For an illustrative 48-h batch, correct and actionable 2-, 4-, and 8-h forecasts could avoid the same hours of continued operation, equivalent to 4.2%, 8.3%, and 16.7% of time-dependent operating energy relative to waiting for offline confirmation. The framework is thus a proof-of-concept soft sensor and possible input to future model predictive control; independent high-frequency, closed-loop, and industrial validation remain necessary.

title: Integrating end-of-life strategies into product design: A SPEA2-IIV-based closed-loop optimization framework
abstract: Product-configuration decisions determine the feasibility and implementation difficulty of end-of-life (EOL) strategies, yet existing methods often assess EOL only after configuration or handle feasibility through penalty functions. This study develops a hierarchical, traceable closed-loop framework that integrates EOL considerations directly into product-configuration decisions. Four strategy-specific EOL indices for disassembly (DASI), recycling (RCI), disposal (DPI), and remanufacturing (RMI) are propagated from parts through modules and structural units to the product level. Designers select the objectives required for each design task from these indices. The identification-of-individual-validity (IIV) module combines bounded priority repair and post-decoding feasibility auditing to control candidate admission across optimization algorithms. Hierarchical index propagation and IIV thereby connect configuration choices, EOL evaluation, and feasibility control within a unified design process. In the washing-machine case, disassembly and disposal difficulty were minimized, while recycling and remanufacturing indices remained calculated descriptors. The normalized equal-weight ideal-point rule selected P09 as the nominal representative. Relative to the original product, its disassembly and disposal indices decreased by 9.09% and 13.08%, respectively. These reductions indicate fewer appearance–connection barriers and lower material-related disposal difficulty, supporting component separation, recovery, remanufacturing, and cleaner EOL processing. The framework enables designers to trace how part-level choices shape product-level EOL performance and to identify feasible configurations before design decisions are finalized.

title: Enhancing the techno-economic-environmental performance of the catalytic methane pyrolysis process through machine learning-synergized co-design
abstract: The pursuit of sustainable hydrogen production via catalytic methane pyrolysis (CMP) is challenged by the inherent trade-offs among energy efficiency, economic viability, and environmental footprint. To systematically reconcile this sustainability trilemma, this study proposes a novel Machine Learning-synergized, Multi-objective Co-Design (ML-MoCD) framework. The framework establishes a closed-loop workflow integrating exergy-based system diagnosis, data-driven inverse design of the bottleneck unit, and global process optimization. It begins with an exergy analysis of a rigorously validated process model, which quantitatively diagnoses the catalytic reactor as the critical bottleneck of the CMP process, accounting for 85.8% of the total exergy destruction. Targeting the identified reactor bottleneck, the system-level target of minimizing system exergy destruction is then transformed into material-level objectives (maximizing CH4 conversion and H2 yield) to inversely design an optimal catalyst. By integrating the optimized deep neural network model with the improved genetic algorithm, a Pareto-optimal catalyst is successfully inversely designed from a high-dimensional material descriptor space, achieving a balanced high conversion (91.76%) and yield (92.24%). Subsequently, the optimized catalyst is reintegrated into the CMP system, and a high-fidelity surrogate model facilitates the efficient exploration of the global design space. This step yields the three-dimensional Pareto frontier, clearly quantifying the inherent trade-offs among exergy efficiency, unit profit, and specific CO2 emissions. The final implementation of the framework results in a significant performance improvement, with simultaneous improvements of 8.6% in exergy efficiency, 23.7% in profit, and a 49.4% reduction in CO2 emissions compared to the baseline. The proposed ML-MoCD framework offers a generalizable paradigm for the sustainable intensification of complex chemical processes, contributing directly to the goals of industrial ecology and cleaner production.

title: Can AI technology improve well-being with low carbon emissions? Cross-country evidence and club convergence
abstract: Improving well-being while mitigating climate change is a shared challenge for sustainable development, and advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer a possible way to ease this trade-off. Whether AI can deliver both, and under what economic and technological conditions, remains an open question. Using cross-country panel data for 2000–2023, we measure AI development by each country's AI patent knowledge stock, estimate two-way fixed effects models of the relationship between AI and the carbon intensity of well-being (CIWB), and apply the Phillips–Sul method to trace the long-run evolution of CIWB. Growth in GDP per capita is associated with higher CIWB, whereas AI knowledge accumulation is significantly associated with lower CIWB. AI dampens the growth-related rise in CIWB mainly in countries with medium and high AI stocks; by region, the negative association between AI and CIWB is not significant in Asia-Pacific and South Asia or in the Middle East and Africa. Average convergence in CIWB coexists with long-run divergence across paths, and we identify three internally convergent CIWB clubs. Low and rapidly improving CIWB paths are concentrated in countries with strong initial economic and technological endowments, fast AI development, and relatively weak pressure from economic expansion. AI is associated with lower carbon intensity of well-being, but the association depends on economic foundations, energy structure, and development conditions. The findings offer a new perspective on the sustainability effects of AI and on why they differ across countries.

title: Phyto-mediated synthesis of CuO nanorods for miniaturised electrochemical phenol sensing in water quality monitoring
