title: Exploring a Shared Augmented Reality Experience for Co-Located Co-Design and Maintenance on the Shop Floor.
abstract: Industrial maintenance plays a critical role for operational efficiency, prolonging equipment lifespan, and minimizing unplanned downtime that can disrupt production workflows. Incorporating co-design practices into this domain is equally important, as it facilitates the development of tools and processes that are better aligned with how maintenance procedures are actually carried out. Augmented Reality (AR) technologies have proven effective in supporting such scenarios, enhancing training, and reducing downtime. Nevertheless, in such contexts, certain tasks require a coordinated team effort, fostering a collaborative approach where multiple technicians work together to diagnose issues, share insights, and implement solutions efficiently. Yet, most AR studies focus on individual assistance, validated under controlled laboratory settings with simplified scenarios that do not accurately represent real-world challenges. This work proposes a collaborative AR tool that enables various co-located technicians to interact synchronously. The tool facilitates shared 3D object manipulation, decomposition of complex models, precise measurements, and sketching annotations for effective communication. These features establish a common ground among team members, ensuring a unified understanding of the task at hand. As a use case, a heavy hydraulic press was considered, a crucial component of the production line, selected following a Human-Centered Design (HCD) methodology in collaboration with industry partners. The tool was validated through iterative testing with maintenance technicians and Industry 4.0 engineers, ensuring alignment with real-world needs and expectations.

title: Simulating End-to-End Hand-Sewn and Stapled Anastomosis in a Virtual Colorectal Surgical Trainer.
abstract: Open colorectal anastomosis remains difficult to support in virtual reality due to the need for unconstrained bimanual interaction and realistic soft-tissue behavior. We present the Virtual Colorectal Surgical Trainer (VCoST), a unified physics-based VR framework supporting both end-to-end hand-sewn anastomosis (VCoST-ETEHSA) and linear stapled anastomosis (VCoST-LSA). The system integrates deformable bowel models, phase-based procedural control, tracked instruments, and continuous performance logging. We evaluated VCoST-LSA with 24 participants (12 experts, 12 novices). Total rubric scores did not differ significantly between groups, though experts received higher scores, completed the task faster, and showed improved early bowel stabilization. Workload ratings indicated generally low-to-moderate perceived workload across subscales. While univariate kinematic metrics were not significant, multivariate analysis suggested dominant variability related to motion smoothness. Taken together, these findings suggest that VCoST-LSA captures complementary process-level kinematic signals that complement aggregate rubric scores; however, this initial study does not establish construct validity and motivates larger, confirmatory evaluations.

title: A Hybrid Architecture for Low Latency AR Alignment.
abstract: Multi-user Augmented Reality (AR) systems are critical for the enhancement of existing and future collaborative robotic systems. Multi-user systems provide information that may otherwise be unavailable to an independent user and augmented reality enables the integration of that information naturally into the human perception system. Multi-user AR systems can scale large, become complex, and generate quantities of data that must be managed and communicated between users. This paper describes efforts to lower human perceived end-to-end latency of a multi-user AR system. The system is measured with respect to user perceived latency as a motivation for directing efforts for future system-level research as well as improvements. We find that the latency bottleneck is associated with the cloud server based user alignment system. We augment the system with a peer-to-peer alignment scheme that runs in parallel to the cloud server based alignment. We implement the new user alignment system and measure latency and user alignment accuracy with respect to the user expected cloud server alignment. Finally we analyze data from experiments conducted with the fully implemented system. We find that the peer-to-peer hybrid system along with our proposed gravity-based alignment drastically reduces user perceived latency at the cost of some variance in positional and angular accuracy. We discuss future work on how the system may be made more robust to scaling and network conditions.

title: Dreaming of Butterflies.
abstract:
Dreaming of Butterflies is a mixed reality installation that examines how understanding can emerge through perception rather than instruction. A butterfly guides visitors from a quiet tea room through three interconnected scenes and back again, shaping attention through subtle pacing and minimal gestures such as gentle reach and slow turn. The work explores how perceptual orientation shifts when meaning arises through embodied sensing instead of explicit direction. The installation runs on Apple Vision Pro with a real-time ink rendering pipeline and is presented within a 
3×3
 meter seated tea room environment. It investigates the relationship between guidance, attention, and embodied experience in mixed reality.

title: Investigating Psychological Value-Based Decision Making in Virtual Reality.
abstract: Psychological value-based decision making has been widely studied in traditional laboratory and real-world contexts, yet these approaches often lack ecological variability and immersive engagement. Virtual Reality (VR) offers a unique opportunity to simulate complex, dynamic environments that can reveal underlying mechanisms of value-driven choices. This ongoing project aims to examine how psychological values, such as perceived trustworthiness, intelligence, and physical attributes, influence decisionmaking processes, including choice and reaction time, in immersive VR scenarios. Participants will complete a series of forced-choice tasks embedded in realistic virtual contexts, with eye-tracking data collected to assess attentional patterns. By leveraging VR's flexibility, this study seeks to expand current models of value-based decision-making and to provide insights applicable to domains such as hiring, consumer behavior, and moral judgment.

title: Hydra - a Hybrid Controller for Multi-Haptic Feedback to Mimic Impulsive Forces in Virtual Reality.
abstract: In this project, we envision a versatile Virtual Reality (VR) controller to create haptic illusions for impulsive force scenarios where an active haptic device is essential. The HYbriD contRoller for multi-hAptic feedback (HYDRA) combines force feedback based on airflow with instantaneous tactile feedback realized through a magnetically accelerated weight. To address challenges in the application of brushless motors for force feedback, we propose using toroidal propellers in conjunction with options to adjust the motor layout. For an early pilot study, a Role-Playing Game (RPG) scenario was developed, where, based on a haptic illusion, HYDRA mimicked a 16th-century matchlock musket. With 24 participants, the potential of HYDRA was visible in terms of usability and presence response, as well as promising directions for future studies examining the influence of both feedback types on the experience.

title: Scalable Portals for Distant Object Manipulation in Virtual Reality.
abstract: Portal-based interaction supports distant object manipulation in Virtual Reality (VR) by bringing remote content into the user's reachable space, but its effectiveness is often limited by sensitivity to object scale. In this work, we examine scalable portal designs that reduce scale-related limitations in portal-based interaction. We explore two designs: a single scalable portal with explicit user control of scale and a dual-portal approach that decouples selection and manipulation through automatic scale normalization. A preliminary pilot user study using a 3D docking task suggests that both scalable portal designs reduce mean task completion time compared to a static portal baseline, particularly for smaller targets, while introducing modest selection overhead.

title: Feet in the Sand: Unlock the Restorative Power of the Sea through Virtual Activities.
abstract: This research explores Mixed Reality (MR) ocean blue spaces to support mental wellbeing among adolescents and young adults, a group vulnerable to mental health disorders [1], when physical ocean access is limited. While natural blue space activities boost health outcomes [2], art-based virtual water experiences remain underexplored for those restricted by location, illness, or mobility. We propose a non-gamified seaside intervention set at Taputeranga Marine Reserve, featuring multi-sensory coastal soundscapes, immersive hand-triggered exploration, guided dance with breathing exercises, and ocean reconnection. Unlike passive VR relaxation, this approach emphasizes active movement, cultural resonance, and place-memory evocation. Cross-cultural workshops planned for Wellington, Aotearoa New Zealand and Busan, South Korea (2026) will evaluate emotional responses, stress relief, and therapeutic potential through multimodal participant feedback. Ethical review is underway to assess learnability, visual cueing, and embodiment risks.

title: Extending Motion Complexity Reduction with Eye Gaze Data to Evaluate Cybersickness.
abstract: The measurement of cybersickness levels in research are often subjective reports which are prone to reporting bias, creating a need for objective measures. Recent work has proposed motion complexity, using the d95 metric, based on principal component analysis of head movement data, as a potential objective indicator of cybersickness. This study examines the robustness of the d95 metric under constrained motion conditions and examines the utility of including eye tracking data. d95 scores were computed using six degrees of freedom from head movement data (d95.6) and nine degrees of freedom by extending to explore the use eye gaze data (d95.9). While both metrics showed significant relationships with FMS sickness scores when analyzed independently, neither remained significant when analyzed in the combined model where the study's experimental condition was the only significant predictor. Analysis of principal component loadings revealed that translation was the dominant modality in the first principal component, while eye movements were dominant in the second and third principal components. However, translation remained the dominant modality by total variance explained across the three principal components. These results suggest that extending d95 to eye tracking does not improve predictive power and that d95 primarily reflects head movement rather than fine oculomotor behavior.

title: Addressing Personalized Virtual Reality for Stroke Rehabilitation Through a Country Fair Serious Game Approach: A Proposal.
abstract: Traditional rehabilitation for stroke survivors adopt uniform approaches, which can reduce motivation, engagement, and the effectiveness of recovery. This paper introduces a Personalized Virtual Reality (VR) experience for Stroke Rehabilitation through a Country Fair serious game approach. The rehabilitation takes the form of a virtual fairground composed of multiple tents, each hosting a distinct activity. These will be designed with customizable parameters, e.g., task difficulty, movement range, or cognitive demands, that can be adapted by healthcare professionals to match each survivor. The metaphor of a country fair also adds an engaging dimension. Survivors can explore diverse experiences that feel playful, varied, and never repetitive. This adaptability can foster sustained participation, increase the sense of agency, and align rehabilitation with the survivor's evolving progress. The paper defends the benefits of personalized VR in stroke recovery, outlines the potential of the Country Fair approach, and identifies directions for future research and development.

title: Text-Guided 3D Object Extraction from 360° Tours: from Panoramas to Interactive VR Experiences.
abstract: Museums are stepping up their efforts to digitize their historical, artistic, and culturally significant collections. Since only a fraction can be physically displayed, virtual reality (VR) expands access to these artifacts while offering visitors richer and more engaging experiences, which benefit both institutions and curators. In this context, this work proposes an end-to-end approach to create a custom and interactive VR experiences through virtual exhibitions. Using 360° panoramas and plain-language prompts, artifacts from real museum exhibitions are generated and assembled into a virtual museum, enabling customized and interactive VR experiences. Additionally, a retrieval-augmented generation technique is employed to provide grounded, object-scoped explanations. In a pilot evaluation, outcomes on user interaction were promising, suggesting that the scene aided participants in a immersive guidance and enabled artifact comprehension. Overall, our study demonstrates promising results in transforming static 360° tours into interactive, guided VR galleries, making way for richer experiences in virtual museums.

title: Frequent Subjective Assessment in Virtual Reality Based on Click.
abstract: In virtual reality user studies, questionnaires are commonly used to collect subjective data but rely on retrospective reporting, limiting their ability to capture in-experience variations. We propose a method for frequent in-game subjective assessment based on a simple controller button click. As a use case, participants reported their self-efficacy before each shot in a virtual ball-throwing task. Results show a statistically significant positive correlation between the click-based and questionnaire-based measures, indicating the potential of this approach for future virtual reality studies.

title: Looping 3D Videos From a Moving Camera Via Recycled 2D Tracking.
abstract:
We present a system for generating looping 3D videos from casual monocular footage captured by a single moving camera. Unlike existing looping 3D video methods that rely on a stationary multicamera system, our approach synthesizes multi-camera views to mimic a physical multi-camera setup. Our key technical contribution is the efficient construction of all-pairs long-term 2D tracking by reusing multi-step optical flow, which avoids the need for expensive pairwise tracking. Our approach is 122.8 times faster than the pairwise approach while maintaining 
98.2,99.5
, and 99.7 % of the visual quality in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, respectively.

title: Effects of Multisensory Feedback and Real-World Priming on Presence and Copresence in Mixed Reality Drone Simulation.
abstract: Virtual reality (VR) experiences often rely on multisensory cues and realistic interactions to support convincing interpretations of virtual events and agents. This study examines how two factors, real-world priming and multisensory feedback, shape users' perceptions of a virtual drone in a mixed-reality simulation. We conducted a mixed-design experiment where participants experienced either a physical drone flyover or no physical drone encounter, followed by audiovisual and multisensory drone flyovers in VR. Multisensory feedback increased co-presence and perceived realism specifically for participants who had encountered the real drone. In contrast, neither manipulation significantly affected standard presence measures. These findings highlight distinctions among presence-related constructs and suggest that recent real-world experiences can make certain multisensory cues be perceived as more realistic, even when they do not increase presence itself.

title: Zero-Shot and Foundation Model Performance on Face Emotion Recognition for Avatars in XR - Challenges, Limitations, and Potentials.
abstract: Avatars are increasingly used as primary user representations in XR systems, making accurate interpretation of their emotional expressions essential for inclusive and trustworthy human-computer interaction. However, facial emotion recognition (FER) models are predominantly trained on real-faces, and their behavior on avatarlike representations remains poorly understood due to the lack of annotated avatar emotion datasets. In this work, we systematically evaluate two approaches: a pre-trained FER model (HSEmotion) trained on real-face data, and a large-scale foundation model (CLIP) without task-specific fine-tuning. We assess their performance on both real-face (FERV-39k) and avatar-like (FaceExpressions-70k) datasets. Using labeled real-face data and expression-emotion mappings from the literature, we analyze model behavior, performance differences, and sources of uncertainty in avatar-based settings. Our results show that emotion-specific models exhibit stronger alignment with established expression-emotion relationships, while foundation models face limitations in fine-grained emotion inference. This work supports more transparent and inclusive deployment of affective technologies in XR-systems.

title: From Slides to Space: Interactive Scale Navigation for XR Presentations.
abstract: This paper presents our solution to the 2026 3DUI Contest challenge. Our approach features scale-based navigation and spatialized regions to traverse an immersive presentation, replacing traditional slide decks with embodied movement through a 3D virtual environment (VE). To demonstrate this approach, we designed an immersive presentation centered on the exploration of the solar system, where predetermined regions function as presentation slides. The user, acting as the presenter, exhibits content by scaling and moving the VE over the course of the tour, allowing for both large-scale context and close inspection of details while maintaining clear instructional flow. The system integrates presenteroriented tools commonly used in conventional presentations along with visual and auditory feedback from audience participation. The guided tour provides narrative segments comparable to a presentation slide while allowing attendees to explore current and previously visited regions. This work explores how virtual reality (VR) can extend conventional presentation methods through spatial interaction and embodied navigation.

title: ARMassage: An Augmented Reality System for Learning and Practicing Traditional Chinese Medicine Massage.
abstract: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) massage is well known for its therapeutic effectiveness; however, its training and dissemination are often hindered by a lengthy learning process and high skill-entry requirements. To alleviate these challenges, this paper presents the design and initial implementation of an Augmented Reality (AR)–based system for learning and practicing TCM massage. The proposed system integrates real-time automatic acupoint recognition and calibration, along with visualized feedback of hand-applied pressure on Quest devices, to support more intuitive and guided practice. A preliminary user study was conducted to evaluate the feasibility of the system, through which its current limitations and potential directions for improvement were also identified. The results indicate that incorporating AR technology into TCM massage education can enhance learning efficiency and learner confidence, while providing effective assistance during practical operations. This work demonstrates the potential of immersive technologies to support the modernization and dissemination of TCM massage training.

title: ChromaXR: Enhancing Color Perception for Users with Color Vision Deficiency.
abstract: This demo introduces an extended reality (XR) system designed to enhance environmental perception for individuals with Color Vision Deficiency (CVD). The system leverages a hybrid workflow: first, users perform a digital implementation of the Farnsworth D15 Arrangement Test within a fully immersive Virtual Reality (VR) environment to ensure controlled lighting and diagnostic precision. Based on this assessment, the system generates a personalized visual profile, which is then applied as a tailored, static compensation filter in an Augmented Reality (AR) setting. This overlay optimizes color contrast and discrimination in the user's real-world field of view. At the demonstration venue, participants can experience the full XR pipeline, transitioning from VR-based calibration to ARassisted vision, showcasing the potential of cross-reality tools as scientifically-grounded assistive technologies.

title: Hands-on or Not? Comparing Mid-Air and Passive Haptics in Button-Based VR Training Tasks.
abstract: This pilot study investigates the impact of passive haptics in VR training with simple control elements. 26 participants completed tasks using either mid-air interaction or a physical mock-up providing passive haptic feedback. Learning outcomes were assessed via practical transfer and knowledge tests, and user experience was measured through presence, workload, and usability ratings. No significant differences were found between interaction conditions across any measure. These findings provide initial evidence that, for brief and discrete control-element interactions, passive haptics do not substantially affect performance or experience, guiding future design decisions and studies involving more complex VR training tasks.

title: Designing a Multisensory Embodied Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR) Experience to Explore the Pedagogical Utility of IVR.
abstract: A recent review of studies using Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR) with children found that IVR contributed to positive learning outcomes [7], however a systematic understanding of how each feature of IVR contributes to its success as a learning experience is still limited. This paper outlines the design of a multisensory embodied IVR experience, with the aim to explore how the inclusion of multisensory and interactive features in IVR contribute to the pedagogical success of the experience.

title: Vertical Narrative in Virtual Reality: A Rhythm-Embodiment Design Framework (REDF).
abstract:
VR narratives often prioritize horizontal exploration, leaving vertical experience underexplored. We propose REDF, a Rhythm-Embodiment design framework that treats rhythm as a spatial, embodied experience shaped by users’ movement and the arrangement of graspable elements. REDF supports vertical narrative pacing via (1) post-grasp locomotion-gain modulation for implicit time dilation in information-intensive zones and (2) multi-directional grasp points that encourage body rotation and visual scanning. In a between-subject study 
(N=15)
, information-intensive zones showed longer engagement and higher IPQ presence ratings, supporting REDF as a practical approach for designing vertical narrative experiences in VR.

title: AlgoQuestVR: Interactive VR Puzzles for Learning Sorting Algorithms.
abstract: Conventional algorithm visualizations are largely passive 2D animations; learners can recount steps yet struggle to apply them to novel inputs. Although virtual reality (VR) affords spatial presence and embodied interaction, there is limited work that couples algorithm instruction with interactive practice and code-level grounding. AlgoQuestVR reframes core sorting algorithms as short, replayable VR puzzle levels. A hub world lets learners select Bubble Sort or Quick Sort, and within each algorithm they can enter either a guided “demo” or a more open-ended “puzzle” mode. The learner manipulates a rack of spheres using ray or direct grab, with snapping feedback when values are placed in correct order. A worldspace pseudocode panel highlights the currently executed line in green and explains, in plain English, which elements are being compared and whether they will be swapped. We report formative, in-class user testing with four participants, summarize qualitative feedback, and describe iterations made to improve usability and clarity.

title: Spatial Exploration Behavior in XR Learning: Toward Passive Assessment of Embodied Engagement.
abstract:
Extended Reality (XR) learning environments generate rich behavioral data through embodied interaction-head movements, gaze patterns, and spatial navigation-that could enable passive assessment without interrupting the learning experience. We investigate spatial exploration behavior in ACHIEVE, an XR environment for neural network visualization learning. In a between-subjects study (
N=56
), XR participants exhibited significantly different spatial behavior than desktop users: over 14 times greater pointer movement (
M=132.5 m
 vs. 
M=9.5 m
), extensive head rotation 
(M=9,
818
∘
)
, and 
M=22.5 m
 of head translation during the learning session. We visualize individual exploration patterns through head and pointer trajectory traces, revealing substantial variation in how learners navigate the 3D content. These spatial metrics, automatically captured during learning, represent a promising avenue for passive assessment of embodied engagement-enabling educators to identify struggling learners, provide personalized feedback, and adapt content delivery without intrusive testing. Full learning outcomes and user experience metrics are reported in companion publications; here we focus on spatial behavior as a novel contribution toward spatialized learning analytics in education.

title: Saberception: A Gamified VR Platform for Perceptual Research.
abstract: Saberception is a gamified, immersive VR platform for conducting perceptual experiments under more active and engaging conditions. Inspired by the VR game ‘BeatSaber’, participants slice through oncoming cubes in sync to music. Their performance as a function of stimuli intensity can be used to measure various perceptual thresholds. We demonstrate the utility of the method with a colour discrimination experiment, showing it is possible to rapidly and reliably measure perceptual thresholds during an active task in a fun and engaging manner.

title: GENIE: Generative Narrative Immersion Engine for Deep Reading Engagement.
abstract:
This paper presents GENIE (Generative Narrative Immersion Engine), a virtual reality (VR)-based reading system that generates story-adaptive 360° panoramic environments from narrative text to deepen readers' engagement with fictional stories. To this end, an AI pipeline segments book text into scene-level units, derives location-focused image prompts via large language models, and synthesizes corresponding panoramas using diffusion-based image generation and neural super-resolution models. In a within-subject user study 
(N=32)
 comparing this dynamic environment to a static baseline, we analyzed both subjective Story World Absorption (SWAS) and objective behavior (reading speed, head rotation). The results show that our story-adaptive reading system significantly increased transportation and mental imagery. Moreover, our study reveals critical interaction effects between the narrative and generated environments. These findings suggest that while generative VR can deepen absorption, its effectiveness is modulated by the visual concreteness and pacing of the source text, offering new design implications for the future of immersive reading experiences.

title: Pulling Illusion Induced by Asymmetric Vibration with Visual Motion Cues.
abstract: In this demo paper, we present a VR system that combines vibrotactile feedback with visual motion cues to demonstrate the illusory pulling sensation induced by asymmetric vibration. The demo allows users to experience illusory pulling sensation without applying physical external forces, using a lightweight and ungrounded setup. The system features a simplified visual scene in which object motion provides an interpretable causal context for vibrotactile stimulation. By synchronizing asymmetric or symmetric vibration with object movement, users can directly experience how visual context relates to the perception of pulling sensations. Our demo illustrates design possibilities for illusory pulling sensations supported by visually interpretable motion cues. Conversely, when these cues conflict with users’ expectations, visual causality can weaken the perceived illusion.

title: Virtual Prejudice in Childhood: Impulsive Avoidance Toward Racial Out-Group Avatars.
abstract: Adults maintain larger interpersonal distances from social outgroups due to implicit biases, yet it remains unclear if this emerges in childhood. We utilized Virtual Reality (VR) to investigate personal space regulation in 30 Japanese children (aged 8-16). Participants performed a Stop-Distance Task with avatars varying in race (Asian vs. White), sex (Female vs. Male), and approach direction (Active vs. Passive). Results revealed a significant main effect of race: children maintained larger distances from White (out-group) avatars than Asian (in-group) avatars, suggesting that the implicit biases manifest early in development. Additionally, we found a significant interaction between age and approach direction; while the distance in Passive condition remained stable across all ages, in Active condition, older children approached avatars significantly closer than younger children. These findings suggest that interpersonal distance and approach dynamics may be important considerations when designing VR interactions for children, particularly in contexts involving unfamiliar social agents.

title: Liquid-Gait: Bio-Adaptive AI for Mitigating Virtual Reality Cybersickness on Omnidirectional Treadmills.
abstract: Omnidirectional Treadmills (ODTs) allow infinite locomotion in Virtual Reality (VR) but often induce cybersickness due to sensory conflict. Current static mitigation strategies fail to adapt to dynamic physiological states. We present Liquid-Gait, a bio-adaptive controller using Liquid Neural Networks (LNNs) to modulate translation gain in real-time. By fusing high-frequency ocular telemetry with irregular heart-rate variability, the system avoids the control jitter typical of discrete AI approaches. Preliminary validation indicates the controller acts as a stabilizer, forcing physiological arousal into a bounded limit cycle and reducing accumulated vestibular error compared to static baselines.

title: A Comparison of Heart Rate Visual, Auditory, and Tactile Feedback Modality Design for Relaxation.
abstract: In this study, we explore the design of visual, auditory, and tactile (haptic) heart rate feedback modalities and their combinations within VR settings for relaxation. Our designs help users be immediately aware of their real-time physiological responses. We considered the heartbeat pattern and converted it to three different modalities to represent physiological responses. The collected HR was used in our designed nature-based VR environment to provide a customized heart rate feedback experience. The visual, auditory, and haptic feedback were compared both individually and combined. The outcomes demonstrated that participants preferred the design of auditory and audiovisual modalities. Subjects found these two forms of biofeedback sufficiently realistic to facilitate their awareness of physiological responses within their bodies. The future plan is to improve selected modalities for our relaxing VR setting.

title: Towards Simulating Projector-Based Augmented Reality in Virtual Reality for Interventional Evaluation.
abstract: Evaluating projector-based augmented reality (AR) systems for interventional guidance in clinical environments is costly, timeconsuming, and subject to strict safety constraints. We present a virtual reality (VR)–based simulation approach that enables earlystage evaluation of projector-based AR guidance concepts without requiring physical hardware. A virtual interventional room was created based on a real CT suite and combined with hand-tracked needle interaction and a simulated projector-based guidance visualization. We evaluated the system in a virtual needle insertion task using performance metrics as well as established presence and user experience questionnaires. Results indicate high perceived presence and user experience, while revealing limitations in absolute insertion accuracy. Our initial findings suggest that VR-based simulation is a promising tool for early interventional evaluation of projector-based AR concepts, particularly for usability and user experience studies.

title: Extended Reality for Needle-Based Anesthesia Training: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
abstract: Needle-based procedures in anesthesiology training (e.g., neuraxial puncture and ultrasound-guided regional techniques) require coordinated visuomotor skills and anatomical reasoning. Compared to the total amount of extended reality (XR) studies on anesthesia training and simulation, validation of the effect on needle-based and neuraxial procedures is far less explored. We report on a metaanalysis to evaluate whether XR-based educational interventions improve needle-based procedural performance relative to non-XR instruction. We systematically identified randomized controlled trials or randomized pilot studies and synthesized two outcomes: (1) procedural skill proficiency, measured by Global Rating Scales (GRS), and (2) procedural efficiency, quantified by time-based metrics. Random-effects meta-analyses (standardized mean difference, SMD) are performed for the seven studies meeting the inclusion criteria (4 for proficiency and 3 for efficiency). XR interventions do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (pooled SMD = 0.47, 95% CI[-0.21,1.15], p=0.117; I2=0.0%) for procedural skill proficiency; whereas for procedural efficiency, there is a trend toward favoring XR, though not reaching statistical significance (pooled SMD = 0.63, 95% CI [-0.01,1.28], p=0.051; I^{2}=0.0 {\%}). Given the small number of samples, mixed intervention designs, and variability in procedural contexts, the evidence supports consideration of the trend toward efficiency gains with caution, whereas consistent proficiency improvements are not demonstrated.

title: Multimodal Feature Fusion in Mixed Reality for Detection of Neurodegenerative Disorders.
abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's disease involve progressive motor, speech, and balance impairments, whose heterogeneity complicates but underscores the importance of early diagnosis and monitoring. In this study, we present a Mixed Reality (MR)-based framework that leverages Microsoft HoloLens 2 for multimodal, real-time acquisition of behavioral and physiological signals during ecologically valid tasks. We conducted a study involving 137 participants (66 diagnosed with Parkinson's and 71 healthy controls), where MR was employed for both data collection and task presentation. After preprocessing and feature extraction, we applied machine learning models combining deep learning and gradient boosting methods, alongside earlyand late-fusion strategies, to enhance classification performance. Our results indicate that multimodal fusion substantially outperforms single-modality approaches, with early fusion reaching high performance on both accuracy and F1-score, exceeding 96%. Moreover, MR-based acquisition proved alternative to conventional smartphone- and smartwatch-based systems by enabling synchronized, multidimensional, real-time data capture across multiple modalities.

title: Year of the Cicadas.
abstract: Year of the Cicadas is an autoethnographic virtual reality experience that explores how parental grief changes over time. The work is rooted in the co-creator's loss of her six-year-old son in 2004 and the Brood X cicada emergence that followed. When the cicadas returned seventeen years later, their predictable cycle became a way to reflect on how grief reshapes itself, resurfaces, and becomes part of the story a person carries forward. The installation includes a memorial component where visitors write the name of someone they have lost on a small paper cicada and hang it on a tree sculpture.

title: COGNIAUDIT: Cognitive Load-Aware Auditory Feedback for Balance Control in Virtual Reality.
abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) systems are very useful for decision-making, training, and rehabilitation. However, their complex, multimodal settings frequently impose significant cognitive and balance difficulties. Excessive auditory, visual, and sensory stimulation can overwhelm users, impairing balance and performance and limiting the accessibility of extended reality (XR) technology. This pilot study examines the strategic design and investigation of helpful auditory feedback to mitigate cognitive load and improve balance in immersive settings. This research enhances the fundamental knowledge that auditory feedback can reduce cognitive load, with statistical analysis confirming this improvement $(p=.0011)$ and improve balance in VR, providing realistic design guidelines for accessible and inclusive immersive technologies. The result also demonstrates how the body balance affects cognitive load, which helps to make XR experiences safer and more useful for everyone.

title: VR-CivicGuard: Enhancing Campus Civil Defense and Air Defense Preparedness Through Immersive Virtual Reality Training.
abstract: As drones and missile strikes become major threats in modern warfare, traditional civil defense training often fails to build the procedural memory required for survival. We present VRCivicGuard, an immersive VR simulation that trains users in expert-informed air raid standard operating procedures. Developed through interviews with civil defense specialists, the system targets critical survival skills, including blast-mitigation posturing, emergency item collection, debris navigation, and drone evasion. A pilot study showed high usability and immersion, and participants trained with VR-CivicGuard significantly outperformed a control group. These findings highlight the effectiveness of expertinformed VR for civil defense training.

title: RepSync: Real-Time Form Correction and Feedback in Virtual Benchpress Training.
abstract: Improper bench press posture increases injury risk and reduces training efficiency. We present RepSync, a VR-based coaching system providing real-time multimodal feedback for posture correction. By integrating wearable Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) and wireless EMG, RepSync monitors limb kinematics and muscle activation. The system evaluates form based on forearm verticality and elbow abduction, delivering corrective visual cues via an immersive dashboard. By projecting physiological data into the user's field of view, RepSync enables self-correction of biomechanical errors without external supervision. Preliminary results indicate that the system effectively mitigates common technical faults for both novice and experienced lifters.

title: An Immersive Serve Type Recognition Skill Training System for Table Tennis Beginners.
abstract: Learning to identify serve spin is a fundamental yet challenging skill for table tennis beginners because the relevant motion cues are subtle and often difficult to observe in traditional training settings. We present an immersive system that reconstructs realistic serve motions from multi-view videos and provides flexible viewpoints, self-directed practice, and visualization tools that reveal essential spatiotemporal cues. The system enables learners to explore serve motions interactively within a virtual environment. A study with novice participants illustrates the promise of this approach for supporting early-stage perceptual learning in table tennis training.

title: "Body Oracle" Translator.
abstract: What if your body posture and movement could be read as a sentence? “Body Oracle” Translator is a handheld mixed reality device that translates human body postures and movement into speculative AI-generated hieroglyphic characters in real time. This computational linguistic speculative design project creates an alternative language system inspired by Chinese Oracle-Bone Inscriptions, promoting cross-cultural collective bodily awareness in an era dominated by language-based communication. Glimpsing through the lens, users inhabit an “alternative present”—one where these hieroglyphic characters have existed for thousands of years—where this alternative language reshapes our understanding of the body and influences collective body awareness.

title: FeltSight.
abstract: FeltSight is a mixed reality haptic experience that reimagines human perception by drawing inspiration from the tactile navigation of the star-nosed mole. Moving beyond traditional, visiondominated interaction paradigms, FeltSight enables users to engage in meditative wandering guided by extended-range haptics with subtle visual cues. The system comprises a wearable haptic glove paired with an extended reality interface. As users reach toward objects in their environment, the glove's vibration actuators—driven by audio-responsive patterns—simulate material textures, producing a sensation akin to touch. Meanwhile, the mixed reality interface offers a deliberately “reduced reality”, presenting nearby objects as dynamic point clouds that materialize only in response to exploratory hand gestures. By shifting perceptual focus from the visual to the tactile, FeltSight challenges ocularcentric sensory hierarchies and foregrounds an embodied, relational, and more-thanhuman mode of sensing.

title: Conducting Questionnaire Interviews in Virtual Reality Using an Intelligent Virtual Agent.
abstract: Collecting rich qualitative feedback in virtual reality (VR) remains challenging. While standardized questionnaires can assess presence, VR sickness, or user experience using 2D user interfaces (UI) in 3D space, obtaining detailed open-ended responses requires cumbersome text entry, which researchers often avoid. We present and evaluate a novel approach using a large language model (LLM)driven intelligent virtual agent (IVA) that conducts spoken questionnaire interviews in VR. In a within-subjects study (\mathrm{N}=36), we compared an IVA interviewer to a conventional in-VR 2D-UI questionnaire, administering both the Igroup Presence Questionnaire (IPQ) and open-ended questions. The results demonstrate that the IVA reliably collects data without systematic measurement distortion in Likert scales, elicits 3.5 \times longer and more diverse free-text responses, and reduces workload for open-ended questions while trading off efficiency for closed items. Our findings establish LLM-driven IVAs as a viable and advantageous survey modality for VR research, particularly for collecting rich qualitative feedback that traditional methods struggle to capture. We discuss design implications and provide recommendations for when IVA-based questionnaires offer the greatest benefit.

title: WebGPU-Accelerated Multimodal Content Generation for Immersive XR Presentations.
abstract: We present a novel system that reimagines how users create and deliver presentations within extended reality (XR). Beyond static 2D slides, our approach enables presenters to generate images or 3D objects dynamically using natural language input, supporting immersive storytelling and interactive Q&A in real time. The system leverages a modular architecture combining voice or text input, a WebGPU-enabled frontend for local AI inference, and a backend MCP-based pipeline for text-to-image-to-3D generation. The prototype demonstrates how presenters can create museum-like or spatially rich presentations, respond to unexpected questions with new visualizations, and explore spontaneous content generation within an XR environment.

title: MirroringWay: Designing an Inter-World Transition Method with Materialized Mirror Imagery.
abstract: This study explores a novel transition method for enabling experiences that traverse multiple types of worlds, including real, virtual reality (VR), and augmented reality (AR). As such an approach, we designed MirroringWay, a transition method that employs a mirror as the mediating element. MirroringWay reproduces within VR mirror-generated imagery resembling an endlessly extending space produced by a facing-mirror configuration and materializes it as a traversable transition space. In this paper, we conducted a demooriented user study focusing on experiences that involve transitions across multiple heterogeneous spaces. The results suggest that Mirroring Way enables spatial transitions to be understood as a reasoned movement experience and has the potential to endow the transition itself with meaning and enjoyment.

title: Exploring Foot Pressure Sensing for Avatar Manipulation and for Input Modality in VR.
abstract: Avatar manipulation is a fundamental component of virtual reality (VR) systems, as it enables immersive user experiences and supports natural and expressive interaction. Foot pressure sensing is as a promising alternative input for lightweight and unobtrusive. Because foot-ground interaction naturally occurs during common VR activities such as standing, walking, and weight shifting, pressure-based signals can be captured with minimal instrumentation while encoding rich information about whole-body dynamics. These properties make foot pressure sensing particularly well suited for VR scenarios that prioritize seamless integration, user comfort, and embodied interaction. In this paper, we extend dataset to more variety of motion and group them into four categories, hand manipulation, squat and jump, arm swing and locomotion. Then, we trained transformerbased network model. We analyzed accuracy by each category. We observe that hand pose estimation is consistently less accurate than lower-body estimation, with errors becoming more pronounced during rapid movements. This degradation is likely due to the combination of high motion velocity, limited sensing coverage for the upper body, and the absence of direct force-based signals for the hands. Finally, we propose three application of VR with foot pressure sensor that span input, embodiment, and skill training. Specifically, we employ pressure signals as a hands-free input modality for both discrete and continuous control, enable full-body avatar manipulation through pressure-based pose estimation without extensive upper-body instrumentation, and support sports-oriented interaction by analyzing lower-body weight transfer during baseball swing practice. Together, these applications illustrate how foot pressure sensing can facilitate expressive, unobtrusive, and contextaware avatar manipulation across diverse VR scenarios.

title: Effects of VR Visual Feedback on the Perceptual Characteristics of Tendon Vibration-Induced Kinesthetic Illusion.
abstract: Kinesthetic illusion is a promising technique for providing proprioceptive feedback in neurorehabilitation and virtual reality (VR). However, reliable methods for inducing strong illusions remain unclear. This study investigates the effect of VR-based visual feedback on kinesthetic illusion perception. A virtual right hand moving in accordance with the kinesthetic illusion is presented via a head-mounted display and compared with an eyes-closed condition. The results show that illusion perception is enhanced by synchronized virtual hand feedback, with statistically significant differences observed under specific experimental conditions, indicating that VR visual feedback effectively modulates the strength of kinesthetic illusions.

title: A Gaze Guidance Approach for Specialized Skill Training and its Effect on Trainees Gaze Patterns.
abstract: Efficient acquisition of gaze patterns is indispensable for improving specialized skills yet learning such patterns typically requires extensive time, repeated practice, and expert support. This paper proposes a gaze guidance approach for specialized skill training based on two visual designs, Flicker and Mask, which present guidance during practice to promote more efficient gaze behavior, and evaluates their effects on trainees gaze patterns. We evaluate the effects of these approaches on trainees gaze patterns in a virtual reality training environment. The results suggest that training time gaze guidance using Flicker and Mask can locally stabilize gaze behavior, but its benefits may be limited only in the training time and may not persist without continued support.

title: Object-Centric Sampling for 3D Object Detection via Pseudo Labels.
abstract: Point cloud-based 3D object detection has become a core technology for 3D scene understanding in various fields, including autonomous driving, robotics, and augmented reality. In indoor 3D object detection, random sampling is commonly applied to input points to control the model's input size. However, this approach often fails to preserve sufficient object points, which typically occupy a much smaller proportion compared to background points such as walls and floors. This randomness leads to performance instability and variability across different trials. To address these issues, we propose a pseudo label-based Object-Centric Sampling Module. Specifically, we utilize a pretrained segmentation model to obtain panoptic segmentation-based pseudo labels and determine the sampling ratio between object and non-object points through a weighted average strategy. This design maximizes the preservation of object information while maintaining an appropriate amount of background points necessary for capturing the global context of the scene. Overall, our method effectively addresses the limitations of random sampling in point cloud-based 3D object detection.

title: VIRTOSHA - A VR Training Simulation for Osteosynthesis Procedures with Force Feedback and Tissue Simulation.
abstract: Osteosynthesis training requires development of force-sensitive manual skills and an understanding of workflows, which are difficult to acquire through theoretical instruction or cadaver-based training. While Virtual Reality (VR) offers new opportunities for surgical training, existing systems often focus on isolated subtasks, lacking integrated support for realistic interaction, procedural logic, and adaptability. This paper presents a work-in-progress VR training system designed for workflow-oriented osteosynthesis training. The system combines force feedback, physics-based tissue simulation and robust hand tracking in a modular architecture. Additionally, an expert-driven authoring workflow enables medical professionals to define and adapt training scenarios without programming. Using a reference scenario for fibular fracture osteosynthesis, we describe the system design, core components, and current implementation status. We further discuss technical trade-offs, limitations, and directions for future validation. Our system establishes a foundation for force-sensitive, workflow-oriented VR training and serves as a basis for future studies in surgical education.

title: Enhancing Accommodative Function in XR via Dynamically Modulated Peripheral Chromatic Blur.
abstract: Extended reality (XR) displays require users to view content at near distances for extended periods, leading to sustained ciliary contraction that may induce eye fatigue, pseudomyopia, and presbyopia. We propose a method that dynamically alternates peripheral chromatic defocus blur based on the principle of longitudinal chromatic aberration, aiming to train and enhance accommodative function during XR use without users perceiving the blur. We conducted refraction and accommodative tests, along with subjective assessments, to evaluate this approach. The method improved accommodative facility and reduced near-to-far latency, suggesting that dynamic chromatic blur can enhance accommodative function without being perceptually noticeable to users.

title: Perceptual Thresholds of Sample Counts in AI-Augmented 3D Gaussian Splatting.
abstract: Image-based 3D reconstruction methods such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) are increasingly used to enable real-time freeviewpoint navigation in VR/AR, but achieving accurate texture and geometry typically requires dense multi-view captures. Recent generative models can synthesize additional training views from sparse inputs, yet it remains unclear how many generated views are needed and when augmentation helps or even degrades for 3DGS training for the perceived quality of 3DGS rendering. We conduct a perceptual user study that varies the number of captured and AI-generated images for 3DGS training, and identify perceptual thresholds: adding generated views improves plausibility and visual quality when real images are scarce, but provides diminishing or negative returns once real-view coverage becomes sufficient.

title: Deployment of Web-Based Immersive VR in a Korean Elementary Classroom: A Field Study on Earth and Moon Movements.
abstract: Teaching abstract concepts like Earth and Moon movements is challenging in K-12 education due to the difficulty of observing celestial phenomena directly. To address this, we integrated a web-based VR curriculum, which was initially developed and recognized for its educational efficacy in a national research project [7], into a Korean elementary science classroom, combining tablet-based interactions with stereoscopic viewing via a smartphone-based HMD (Google Cardboard). A field study with 48 sixth-grade students compared this VR approach against traditional instruction. Results indicate the VR group achieved statistically significant gains in scientific attitude (t=2.61, p=.012) and self-directed learning (Q1-Q5; all items p<.05). This study demonstrates the practical viability and educational effectiveness of deploying accessible VR courseware in real-world school settings.

title: Does AI's Personality Matter? Comparing Verbally Extraverted and Introverted AI-Driven Guides in a VR Museum Experience.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can compliment cultural heritage learning within personalized guided virtual tours. This research explores agent traits that embed personality types, specifically verbal extraversion, to examine their impact on users' experience. Utilizing a VR museum of Chinese bronze chime bells as the experimental platform, the study employs systematic linguistic modulation to vary the AI guide's personality while maintaining visual and technical consistency. Through a between-subjects experiment (N=30), we analyzed how these personality-driven traits shape psychological immersion and knowledge acquisition. Our findings reveal critical trade-offs between guidance styles, demonstrating that extraverted traits significantly foster emotional resonance and active participation. This work extends agent design theory into the VR domain, providing an actionable design strategies for personality-embedded AI guides in cultural education.

title: On the Feasibility of Eog-Based Eye-Writing in Virtual Reality.
abstract: Virtual reality (VR) offers immersive environments for exploring gaze-based input modalities beyond conventional hand- or controller-based interaction. This work investigates the feasibility of electrooculography (EOG)-based eye-writing as a gaze-based interface in VR, addressing limitations of prior monitor-based approaches that restrict natural movement. We developed a VR-guided acquisition system integrating a customizable VR interface with a desktop-based measurement application for synchronized EOG data collection. Using this system, we collected EOG data from 18 participants performing digit eye-writing tasks (0-9). Our results show that VR-based acquisition can capture meaningful EOG patterns corresponding to eye-writing gestures.

title: AIs or Humans in Luxury Shopping? A Design Study of VR Shopping Assistants.
abstract: This study investigates four shopping assistant types (3D avatar, webcam, AI, voice) in VR luxury environments through user studies with 20 participants using NASA-TLX, questionnaires, and interviews. Results show 3D avatar assistants excelled in immersion, trust, and satisfaction, while human-operated assistants outperformed AI in realism and satisfaction. Webcam achieved 50% immersion preference versus 75% for 3D avatars despite strong trustworthiness. The study pioneers PC-VR asymmetric interaction systems, providing design insights and optimization strategies for luxury retail VR shopping assistants.

title: Fine-Grained Spatial Scene Reconstruction for Adaptive Memory in Virtual Reality.
abstract: Human spatial memory is reconstructive rather than veridical, relying on partial cues, prior knowledge, and iterative refinement. Existing XR memory systems largely emphasize capture fidelity and replay, offering limited support for this constructive process. We present a VR system that frames spatial memory recall as interactive scene reconstruction through explicit editing operations. The system treats a remembered environment as an editable spatial artifact, supporting insertion, movement, cloning, and deletion of scene elements. A hybrid approach combines a 360 panorama as an egocentric contextual scaffold with manipulable 3D objects for fine-grained spatial adjustment, alongside localized panorama editing for correction and suppression of background elements. By operationalizing reconstruction as a sequence of visible edits rather than passive playback, this work provides a foundation for studying how XR tools shape remembered spatial scenes and supports future behavioral evaluation within the XRMemory context.

title: Can We Have Both? Balancing Agency and Attention in Route-Guided, Focused VR Experiences.
abstract: VR locomotion often entails a trade-off: active control enhances user agency but can divert attention from content, whereas passive travel supports focused viewing at the cost of autonomy. We investigated whether semi-active control can mediate this dichotomy by comparing active, passive, and semi-active locomotion in a user study (N = 24) conducted in a structured, route-guided VR museum. Eye-tracking analyses showed that semi-active locomotion sustained exhibit-focused visual attention at a level comparable to passive travel, while subjective agency remained comparable to active control. These findings suggest that minimal, intentional input can effectively balance agency and attention in focused, predefined VR experiences.

title: Exploring the Role of Contextual Belief in Sensory Integration and Motion Sickness for In-Car VR.
abstract: In in-car virtual reality (VR), ambiguous vehicle-related non-visual signals may increase reliance on top-down interpretation. We conducted a pilot study in a stationary vehicle using a headset-delivered low-frequency tone as a controllable surrogate cue, and manipulated instruction context to frame it as either aligned with VR forward motion (Aligned) or unrelated background (Not-Aligned). Phase 1 varied onset asynchrony to estimate temporal binding windows, and Phase 2 used a fixed asynchrony during repeated exposure to probe perceived coherence and motion sickness. This design offers an initial testbed for examining how contextual framing may shape multisensory inference and discomfort in in-car VR.

title: Virtual Reality and the Affective Gap: Evidence for Immersive Technology as Transitional Support in Undergraduate Science Education.
abstract: Virtual reality (VR) functions as an affective infrastructure in STEM by lowering anxiety, unfamiliarity, and fear of error. Evidence from a randomized trial with first-year chemistry students shows that immersive VR reduces pre-lab anxiety without artificially inflating self-efficacy. Grounded in transition theory, affective learning, and STEM identity research, this paper positions VR as a scalable scaffold that normalizes lab environments, enhances psychological safety, and supports equitable preparation for in-person lab participation and persistence.

title: Work in Progress: Towards Design Criteria for Virtual Humans' Bodily Emotional Gestures in VR Public Speaking Experiences.
abstract: We propose the initial design criteria for the bodily emotional gestures (BEG) of virtual human audiences (VHs) during presentation in a virtual reality (VR) public speaking experiences. Guided by design criteria proposed in earlier studies (approach-avoidance, engaged-distracted, and prototypical audience behaviors), we developed a set of gestures intended to elicit emotions across the four quadrants of the valence-arousal space. Following an initial validation through an online survey $(N=126)$, we identified five emotional bodily behaviors, including a neutral condition, as the most promising for eliciting quadrant-specific emotional responses for future formal evaluation. Based on these findings, this paper discusses the technical details of the BEGs, the next steps for their evaluation, and potential implications.

title: Motion-Based Salient Moment Extraction from 3D VR Training Records for Reflective Learning.
abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) training sessions can be recorded and replayed, enabling immersive after-action review (AAR). However, long-duration VR recordings are costly to review due to combined temporal and spatial exploration overhead. We propose a motion-based salient moment extraction method that operates directly on 3D VR recordings without predefined event logs. The method analyzes object-level transform changes across the scene and extracts representative moments via curve simplification and density-based temporal aggregation. Comparisons with 2D first-personview video summarization show that the proposed 3D method achieves higher recall and robustness, demonstrating its suitability for efficient VR-based AAR.

title: Reducing Heat Dissipation Requirements by Content Brightness Modulation for Lighter Headset.
abstract: Weight reduction in a headset is critical for improving XR usability. This poster investigates whether components related to thermal management (e.g., heat sinks) can be reduced or eliminated, in a PCVR (or thin client type) headset through display brightness and thus temperature modulation. We share findings from several tests, measuring temperature ranges (and differences) among various operating conditions, including the existence of the heat sink, especially on the display. Results have shown a potential for reduction of approximately 2-3 {\%} of weight for the lightest PCVR headset (about 125 g).

title: Asymmetric Telepresence in Sensitive Communication: A Prototype-Based Study on Immersion, Camera Type and Position.
abstract: We introduce a novel asymmetric telepresence system to support sensitive communication circumstances, such as between a therapist and patient in remote counseling. Through the counseling scenario, we conducted a user study with 16 dyads (N=32) participants. In our system, we captured the therapist and their office environment using either a 360° camera or Webcam, and presented it to the patient for an immersive counseling experience. We also tested the camera position on the monitor, either horizontally or vertically. We collected subjective responses regarding the immersive experience quality using questionnaires and eye- and head-tracker data for the Patient (VR group), and collected only subjective responses from the Therapist (PC group). Our findings show a positive impact of the use of an asymmetric telepresence system, particularly when using a 360° camera, in terms of perceived privacy and safety, with sufficient immersion levels for both the Patient and Therapist groups.

title: Beyond the Frame: A Constructivist Framework for Cinematic Education in Immersive VR Environment.
abstract: Virtual reality (VR) is increasingly used in education because it can create embodied learning situations that are difficult to reproduce in physical classrooms. From a constructivist perspective, its value lies less in “presence” than in enabling learners to construct knowledge through situated experimentation. Building on prior VR learning research [3], [4], we present CineSim VR, an experientiallearning environment that lets students enter a virtual film set to rehearse blocking, camera placement, and shot composition. In pilot workshops with media-production students $(n=50)$, participants reported high engagement and that first-person, gesture-based interaction helped them link spatial composition with storytelling intent (Fig. 1).

title: Vibrotactile Mass Cues for Planetary Interaction in VR.
abstract: We present a haptically augmented planetary interaction framework that couples bimanual VR input with procedural multi-actuator vibrotactile feedback on a SenseGlove Nova glove. Our Unity-based environment allows users to beckon, grasp, and rotate virtual planets: the right hand controls global system rotation, and a beckoning gesture that pulls planets toward the user, while the left hand performs direct grasping that triggers tailored vibration profiles across three actuators (thumb and index Linear Resonant Actuators (LRAs) and a wrist-mounted Voice Coil Actuator (VCA)) and grasp-based deformation that distinguishes gaseous from rocky planets. At the core of our design is a command-space model that maps planetary mass and kinematics onto actuator amplitudes and frequencies, together with a pseudo-haptic motion-attenuation scheme that modulates how closely a grasped planet follows the user's hand to reinforce apparent weight and inertia. We introduce a compressed perceptual mass scale that preserves the solar-system mass hierarchy while keeping all planets perceptually discriminable across the available actuator range, and we implement the full pipeline within the SenseGlove Unity SDK. We suggest that this combination of bimanual interaction, command-space mapping, and pseudo-haptic manipulation offers a reusable, purely wearable approach for VR learning environments that require consistent multi-object mass perception and surface cues.

title: CARED-VR: Context-Aware Reinforcement and Enforcement for Drill Training in VR.
abstract: Effective VR safety training needs context-aware regulation during task execution, not just immersive visuals or instructional feedback. We present CARED-VR, a context-aware VR training prototype that integrates a vision-language model (VLM) with haptic gloves to deliver graded reinforcement and enforceable safety constraints in a simulated power-drilling task. The VLM functions as a runtime supervisory layer that evaluates visually observable configurations, including drill-bit and material compatibility and ongoing tool use, against predefined safety conditions. Safe actions proceed uninterrupted, while unsafe configurations trigger a structured escalation of interventions: verbal guidance, simulated physical consequences, and haptic enforcement that physically prevents unsafe operation. We developed CARED-VR, a simulated workshop in which users perform drilling tasks on different materials within a virtual environment (VE) using the SenseGlove Nova 1 in conjunction with a Valve Index headset to enable immersive, haptically augmented interaction. The system illustrates how high-level contextual reasoning can be coupled with low-level embodied interaction to move beyond passive simulation toward execution-time safety control. In addition, CARED-VR serves as a research platform for examining user compliance, workload, and perceived realism.

title: Gaze-Driven User Identification in Affective VR Tasks.
abstract: User identification in virtual reality (VR) is an important capability for personalization, adaptive interaction, and assessment within immersive training and educational systems. Prior works have demonstrated that eye-tracking and physiological signals can support user identification; however, it remains unclear which factors, such as task interaction structure, gaze behavior, and affect-related task cues, most strongly drive identity persistence across tasks in training-relevant VR interactions. In this work, we present a systematic cross-task study of user identification in VR that separates the role of emotional context from interaction structure. Using multimodal eye-tracking and physiological data collected from 33 participants performing four training-relevant affective VR tasks and four structurally matched neutral counterparts, we evaluate identification performance with machine learning and deep learning models. We analyze the effect of task diversity on identification accuracy and examine the relative contribution of eye-tracking and physiological features through explicit modality ablation (eye-only, physiology-only, and fused models). Our results show that user identification performance is largely preserved when affective elements are removed, provided that task structure and gaze behavior remain consistent. Across cross-task settings, eye-tracking features consistently yield more stable and discriminative userspecific signatures than physiological signals, while physiological features provide complementary gains as training spans multiple tasks. Overall, these findings indicate that gaze-driven interaction dynamics play a central role in robust user identification in VR training contexts.

title: Render-to-Display of Analytic Anti-Aliased Text and Vector Graphics in VR.
abstract: Traditional render-to-texture (RTT) approaches struggle to deliver high-fidelity text in VR environments across various scene and display configurations. Analytic anti-aliasing (AAA) achieves supersampled quality at significantly lower computational cost, yet its integration into real-time VR systems remains unexplored. We present an end-to-end render-to-display (RTD) pipeline incorporating AAA for text and vector graphics in VR. Leveraging the Skia 2D library, our system extracts glyph data to analytically compute pixel coverage. Our novel render pipeline for VR demonstrates superior text quality compared to RTT methods, validated through user studies highlighting perceptual improvements.

title: A Quantitative Analysis of Changes in Metaverse Usage Intention as a Third Place Using a Survey with Video Viewing Intervention.
abstract: Metaverse attracts attention as an immersive 3D social space but struggles with widespread daily adoption and retention. While previous studies identified static adoption factors, the procedural transformation of user evaluations through information exposure remains under-explored. Addressing this, we conducted a pre-post online survey with experienced users to quantify changes in continuance intention following an explanatory video intervention. Results indicate significant post-intervention changes in intention. Although effect sizes were modest, evaluation plasticity varied significantly by age: younger and middle-aged groups updated evaluations more readily than seniors. Crucially, the structural relationship between continuance intention and “Third Place” characteristics shifted from experiential and emotional attributes to structural elements supporting sustained usage. These findings imply that information interventions can effectively reconstruct user perceptions, reframing the Metaverse from a temporary novelty into a social space for continuous belonging.

title: Dear Diary, I Won't Give Up My CAVE!
abstract: Daniel F. Keefe is of Professor of Computer Science and Engineering and Director of the Interactive Visualization Lab at the University of Minnesota. Together with other visual computing faculty and students, Keefe's lab recently moved to a custom designed, newly renovated floor of a research building on campus. That is important for this position paper because the move raised the key question: What will happen to the CAVE? After 25 years of working with various large format semi-immersive multi-wall projection screen displays that are both loved and hated for their highperformance visualization capabilities and challenges-the author reflects on the strategy, finances, emotions, interdisciplinary impacts, and technical considerations that have impacted his decision to keep his CAVE alive despite the rapidly evolving landscape of commercially available and more widely supported alternatives for immersive computing. To emphasize the multi-faceted nature of the decision, including the emotion we humans can experience as users and developers of a technology like this, which is almost unique in its ability to both define a physical architectural space and a wide range of complementary virtual spaces, the position paper takes the creative form of a series of entries in a personal diary.

title: CECA - A Configurable Framework for Embodied Conversational AI Agents in Extended Reality.
abstract: We present CECA, a configurable framework for embodied conversational AI agents in Unity-based extended reality (XR) applications. CECA employs a client-server architecture to decouple agent logic from game engine-based embodiment. Built on LiveKit Agents, our approach integrates speech-to-text (STT), large language models (LLMs), and text-to-speech (TTS) into a unified, streaming voice-to-voice pipeline configured via metadata rather than code changes. We outline how this architecture flexibly integrates local and cloud AI providers while mitigating limited provider SDK support in Unity. Finally, we highlight opportunities for future work, including multi-agent scenarios, higher-level templates for XR research, and systematic user studies.

title: DataEcho: Reflective Telemetry Replay for Studying Navigation Strategy Refinement in XR.
abstract: We investigate how persistent telemetry and reflective replay can support navigation strategy refinement in spatial learning tasks in XR. Our approach captures navigation traces, including trajectories, gaze direction, controller input, and interactions, through a Unity package and exposes them in a lightweight browser-based 3D replay interface, enabling post-hoc review without immersive hardware. We evaluated replay-review (interactive 3D replay with gaze visualization) against a no-review control in a controlled study ($\mathrm{n}=25$) with two VR navigation sessions separated by one day. Replay-review led to a significant increase in continuous movement during the second session (greater decisiveness), while backtracking and head-orientation stability showed directional improvements; path optimality did not reliably improve in our lowredundancy layout. These results characterize replay-review as a bundled learner-facing reflection intervention and motivate follow-up studies that isolate the contributions of review baselines and individual replay features. This paper contributes: (1) DataEcho, a platform-agnostic telemetry pipeline supporting secure capture, scalable storage, and browser-based 3D replay of navigation sessions with gaze-ray visualization; (2) a controlled study evaluating replay-review (interactive 3D replay with gaze visualization) versus no review for VR navigation strategy refinement; and (3) limitations and directions for follow-up studies that isolate review baselines and individual replay features.

title: When AR HUDs Become Distractors: Resource-Dependent Memory-Driven Attentional Capture and Design Implications.
abstract: Virtual and augmented reality (VR/AR) systems frequently employ head-up displays (HUDs) to enhance interaction efficiency, yet immersive environments impose substantial demands on working memory (WM) and attention. Information maintained in WM can trigger memory-driven attentional capture (MDAC), diverting attention from external events and increasing the risk of attentional tunneling. This work examines the resource-dependent boundary of MDAC and proposes an XR paradigm to test its generalization to immersive contexts. Behavioral experiments on 2D displays showed MDAC-related performance costs were amplified under high-demand search relative to low-demand search. These findings suggest that in visually complex HUDs, actively maintained WM content can more strongly influence attention, highlighting the need to consider cognitive status alongside display characteristics in immersive interface design.

title: Xrbit: Toward Breaking the Thermodynamic Wall of Persistent LLMs in Mobile XR.
abstract: Deploying persistent Large Language Models (LLMs) on standalone XR devices is fundamentally constrained by the “thermo-dynamic wall,” where on-device processing triggers thermal saturation and cybersickness. While cloud APIs offer an alternative, they impose prohibitive recurring costs for continuous conversational agents and raise privacy concerns regarding sensitive data. To address these barriers without the stochastic latency of cloud offloading, we propose Xrbit, a framework that repurposes a tethered smartphone as a Personal Edge Node. Xrbit employs a Contextual Bandit (LinUCB) offloading agent to dynamically switch between Wi-Fi and BLE, optimizing the trade-off between latency and thermal accumulation in real-time. Evaluations on Meta Quest 3 and Galaxy Z Fold 7 demonstrate that Xrbit sustains stable frame rates (>70 Hz) for 99.85% of the session, effectively minimizing thermal-induced jitter compared to on-device baselines. This work validates that intelligent, thermal-aware edge offloading can enable sustainable, cost-effective, and privacy-preserving always-on AI for mobile XR.

title: With Lily: Design and Implementation of Verbal and Nonverbal Interaction with a Virtual Humanoid in Mixed Reality for Affective Communication.
abstract: This demo presents a virtual humanoid that enables affective communication through verbal and nonverbal interaction in a mixed reality (MR) environment, showcased as an experiential exhibition titled With Lily. The aim of this work is to provide people—who desire social interaction yet feel burdened by concerns such as evaluation or misunderstanding—with a comfortable and enjoyable virtual conversation that is free from real-world social constraints. To this end, the demo implements a comprehensive system that integrates the technical design of verbal and nonverbal interaction for natural emotional and intentional exchange with an augmented virtual presence. The system further incorporates environment design, conversational narrative, and character personality design to foster users’ communication motivation and emotional engagement.

title: Geometry-Aware Scene Configurations for Novel View Synthesis.
abstract: We introduce scene-adaptive strategies for efficiently allocating representation capacity to enable immersive indoor scene rendering. We maximize the use of limited resources, leveraging geometric priors that are typically available after pre-processing. By recording observation statistics on an estimated geometric scaffold, we guide adaptive basis placement, significantly enhancing uniform arrangements used in prior scalable scene representations. We further propose scene-adaptive virtual viewpoints to address geometric deficiencies in input view trajectories and provide effective regularization. Our approach yields substantial improvements in rendering quality over methods based on regular basis placement.

title: Real-Time Physics-Based Force Feedback for VR Simulation in Medicine.
abstract: Tactile feedback in Virtual Reality (VR) is crucial for immersion, yet many systems rely on limited static feedback, reducing training effectiveness, especially in medical simulations. This paper introduces a VR system that utilizes dynamic force feedback through real-time physics calculations.
